The pressure now stretches across some of the country's most recognizable industrial names, touching everything from passenger cars and freight trains to forklifts, aircraft components and factory automation systems.
A Sluggish Economy Feeds Political Discontent

Europe's largest economy has effectively flatlined in recent years, contracting in both 2023 and 2024 before eking out just 0.2% growth last year. Unemployment, at around 4%, remains below the broader European Union average, but that has done little to ease public anxiety over a steady drumbeat of layoff announcements at companies long viewed as pillars of German industry.

Volkswagen has moved to cut roughly 50,000 positions, with reports suggesting further reductions may follow. BMW has outlined plans for 8,000 buyouts by the end of next year, while auto supplier Bosch intends to shed about 13,000 jobs by 2030. Compounding the strain, inflation outpaced wage growth for years after the pandemic, and real wages only returned to their 2019 levels last year.

The economic malaise has become a political liability for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's governing coalition, feeding voter frustration heading into a closely watched regional election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, where the far-right Alternative for Germany party is seen as having a genuine chance at capturing its first state governorship.
From Best Customer to Toughest Competitor

China's shift from a lucrative export market for German goods to a formidable rival has been one of the more consequential turns in the global economy over the past decade. For years, German automakers and machinery makers profited handsomely from selling into China's booming middle class. That dynamic has reversed as Beijing has funneled state support into targeted industrial sectors, many of which directly overlap with Germany's traditional strengths.

With domestic demand in China running well below capacity, manufacturers there have increasingly looked abroad to sell their surplus output, and Europe has absorbed a growing share of it. Volkswagen finance chief Arno Antlitz said the company must bring down its costs at a time when China's overall vehicle market has contracted by roughly a fifth even as Chinese exporters expand their footprint in Europe, intensifying competitive pressure.
Why Germany Has Been Hit Especially Hard

Not every advanced economy has felt the China shock equally. Countries such as Britain, France and Italy carry smaller manufacturing sectors relative to their overall economies, limiting their exposure. The United States, meanwhile, has shielded much of its market through tariffs that block a wide range of Chinese goods, automobiles in particular.

Germany has no such buffer, and the imbalance shows up directly in trade figures: the country now imports more from China than it exports in categories where its manufacturers once led the world, including cars, trucks, buses, trains, aircraft components, factory machinery and medical devices. Economists Brad Setser and Sander Tordoir summarized the shift bluntly, writing that Chinese industry has already consumed much of German manufacturing's advantage and is positioning to erode what remains.
German Firms Respond by Teaming Up With Chinese Manufacturers

Rather than compete head-on across every price point, some German companies are choosing to collaborate with the very manufacturers reshaping their markets. Jungheinrich, a leading German maker of forklifts and warehouse vehicles, has partnered with Chinese manufacturer EP Equipment to produce a lower-cost forklift line called AntOn, designed to compete directly on price.

The arrangement combines EP's large-scale, lower-cost production in China with Jungheinrich's established global sales network and brand reputation. The AntOn machines, distinguished by a bright purple paint scheme rather than Jungheinrich's traditional yellow, strip away some higher-end features, including joystick controls and cushioned seating, in favor of simpler, more basic components, allowing the company to sell them for roughly half the price of its premium equipment.

Nadine Despineaux, the company's chief sales officer, described the strategic dilemma facing German manufacturers as a wave of Chinese products entering both European and international markets, and said the central question for companies is how to respond effectively. She frames the entry-level segment less as a threat than an opening to reach new customers, describing the joint venture as a blend of German engineering and market access paired with efficient Chinese production.

Volkswagen has pursued a related but distinct strategy in China itself, establishing a vehicle development center in Hefei dedicated to designing cars specifically for Chinese consumers, an approach often summarized within the industry as building 'in China, for China.'
Lessons From Germany's Solar Industry Collapse

German officials are acutely aware of how this story can end if left unaddressed. Germany was an early leader in solar panel technology and adoption in the 2000s, but a flood of lower-priced Chinese panels ultimately drove several domestic manufacturers out of business. Today, the majority of solar panels installed in Germany are imported from China, a cautionary precedent policymakers are eager not to repeat in autos and industrial machinery.
How China Built Its Manufacturing Advantage

China's competitiveness rests on more than direct state support, though that support is substantial and includes subsidized credit, discounted raw materials, inexpensive industrial land and, in certain sectors, domestic sourcing requirements. Chinese labor costs also remain considerably lower than in Europe, and economists say the government has worked to keep its currency undervalued, further boosting the price advantage of Chinese exports abroad.

At the same time, analysts note that much of China's manufacturing edge has been forged through intense domestic competition. With China's own economy running below its usual pace, Chinese companies face relentless price pressure at home, pushing them to control costs aggressively and adopt new technology and automation quickly simply to survive in their own market.

China's government rejects the framing of its export growth as a threat to Western economies. A recent report from the country's Ministry of Commerce, titled addressing what it called the 'so-called excess capacity issue,' argued that characterizations of a China shock mischaracterize the country's industrial development as harmful to trading partners.
Germany's Policy Response and the Road Ahead

Berlin has moved on several fronts to try to jump-start growth. The government has established a 500 billion euro, or roughly $579 billion, fund earmarked for infrastructure projects such as roads, bridges and rail lines. A separate package proposed in July includes income tax reductions targeted at middle- and lower-income earners along with efforts to cut regulatory red tape.

Still, some economists argue that the most effective remedies may lie beyond Germany's own borders. Setser, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, contends that trade data points clearly to the China shock as the dominant driver of Germany's economic troubles, and that meaningful solutions increasingly depend on trade policy set collectively by the European Union in Brussels rather than by individual companies or the German government alone.

The European Commission has already imposed targeted tariffs on select Chinese products, including electric vehicles and certain construction lift platforms, though the scope remains narrow relative to the breadth of China's industrial exports. Setser argues that Europe needs a firmer trade posture to insulate its markets from the effects of China's industrial policy, saying the relationship needs to become more balanced so that the rest of the world isn't left fully open to a Chinese economy that restricts imports of its own.

How that balance gets struck will likely shape the next chapter of German industrial policy. For now, companies across the manufacturing sector are left navigating a market where Chinese competitors are no longer simply an emerging threat on the horizon but an established force setting the terms of price and speed that German industry must now match, absorb or work around.

business.metaTitle: Chevron Commits $7B to Expand Venezuela Oil Output
business.title: Chevron to Invest $7 Billion to Expand Venezuela Oil Output
business.metaDescription: Chevron will invest over $7 billion to expand Venezuela operations, aiming to double oil output as the US pushes to unlock the country's vast reserves.
business.excerpt: Chevron has confirmed a multibillion-dollar expansion of its Venezuela operations, adding new acreage in the Orinoco Belt as Washington moves to deepen American access to the country's vast, underdeveloped oil reserves.
business.imageAlt: Oil storage tanks operated by Venezuela's state oil company PDVSA as Chevron expands its Orinoco Belt operations
keyTakeaways: Chevron will invest more than $7 billion over five years to expand its Venezuela operations, aiming to more than double production to about 600,000 barrels a day from roughly 280,000 barrels a day currently.

The expansion follows a broader deal brokered by the Trump administration to open Venezuela's oil sector to US companies, after Venezuela's National Assembly approved the arrangement and US forces captured former President Nicolás Maduro earlier this year.

Venezuela holds the world's largest proven crude reserves at over 303 billion barrels, but analysts warn that reviving the country's neglected oil infrastructure and navigating political risk will take years.

content.text: Chevron confirmed Wednesday that it will pour more than $7 billion into expanding its operations in Venezuela over the next five years, a major bet on a country that holds the world's largest proven oil reserves but has struggled for years to attract the capital needed to develop them. The announcement lands just days after the Trump administration unveiled a sweeping agreement to open Venezuela's oil sector to American companies, an arrangement that also gives the Pentagon a stake in future profits.

The scale of Chevron's commitment underscores how quickly the investment landscape in Venezuela has shifted this year, and it positions the company to significantly expand its already substantial footprint in a country where American energy giants have had little presence for nearly two decades.
What Chevron Announced

Chevron said it has been assigned additional acreage in the Orinoco Belt, the vast region in eastern Venezuela that holds the bulk of the country's extra-heavy crude reserves. The new acreage includes stakes in the Carabobo-1, Carabobo-2-South-A and Ayacucho 8 blocks, which will be folded into Chevron's existing Petropiar joint venture, alongside revised fiscal, commercial and legal terms covering its broader partnerships with Venezuela's state oil company, PDVSA.

Under the plan, Chevron expects to more than double its Venezuelan output, moving from roughly 280,000 barrels a day currently to approximately 600,000 barrels a day. The company said it is targeting production costs of under $20 a barrel, a figure that would keep the investment profitable even if global oil prices soften.

"Chevron's history in Venezuela spans more than a century, and our expanded position reflects our confidence in the country's deep resource potential and its ability to compete for investment within our portfolio for decades," Chevron CEO Mike Wirth said in a prepared statement, adding that the improved terms and additional acreage should help the company deliver low-cost production growth and long-term value.
Why Venezuela's Oil Reserves Matter Globally

Venezuela sits atop the largest proven crude oil reserves of any country on Earth, holding more than 303 billion barrels according to OPEC's most recent annual statistical bulletin, well ahead of Saudi Arabia's 267 billion barrels. Yet despite that enormous endowment, Venezuela's actual output has fallen far short of its potential for years, hampered by aging infrastructure, chronic underinvestment and a wave of departures by international oil companies following the nationalization drive launched under former President Hugo Chávez in 2007.

Chevron was among the few major international producers that chose to remain in the country through that period, accepting minority stakes in PDVSA-controlled joint ventures rather than exiting entirely, as rivals including ExxonMobil and ConocoPhillips did at the time. That decision to stay has now positioned Chevron as the only major US oil company with an established operational presence in Venezuela, giving it a head start as Washington moves to reopen the country to American capital.
The Broader US Push Into Venezuela's Energy Sector

Chevron's expansion is unfolding against the backdrop of a dramatic shift in US-Venezuela relations. Following the capture of former President Nicolás Maduro by American forces earlier this year, Venezuela's National Assembly approved reforms to the country's hydrocarbons law intended to draw foreign investment back into the sector, and it formally approved the broader US-brokered arrangement this week, clearing the legal path for expanded American involvement.

That framework, negotiated by the Trump administration, is reported to give US interests control over roughly a fifth of Venezuela's oil reserves and includes a role for the Pentagon in sharing future profits. The White House has also confirmed a partnership with a company called North American Blue Energy Partners as part of the broader effort to expand US access to Venezuelan crude. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright traveled to Caracas around the time of Chevron's announcement to help finalize related agreements, according to a US official who briefed reporters on condition of anonymity under ground rules set by the White House.

President Trump has pointed to Venezuela's oil wealth as a way to reduce American reliance on Middle Eastern crude, and he has pressed US energy companies to reestablish a presence in the country. He suggested this week that Exxon was also preparing to move into Venezuela, saying, "We have Exxon going in, we have Chevron going in. We have our big oil companies going in." That claim contrasts with earlier remarks from January, when Trump indicated he was inclined to leave Exxon out of the arrangement after CEO Darren Woods described Venezuela as "uninvestable." An Exxon spokesman said this week that the company's position on Venezuela has not changed.
Financial Backing and Investment Capacity

Chevron's ability to fund a multibillion-dollar Venezuelan buildout comes as the company's overall financial performance has strengthened. Chevron reported net income of $12.07 billion for the quarter ended June 30, 2026, with diluted earnings per share of $6.11, a sharp jump from $2.21 billion in net income and $1.11 in diluted earnings per share in the first quarter of the year. Quarterly revenue also climbed, to $67.2 billion in the second quarter from $47.56 billion in the first, according to the company's securities filings. That rebound follows a stretch of comparatively softer quarters through 2025, giving Chevron a stronger financial footing as it commits fresh capital to Venezuela.
Risks Facing Foreign Investment in Venezuela

Despite the scale of the announcement, energy analysts remain cautious about how quickly Venezuela's oil sector can actually recover. Decades of underinvestment have left much of the country's production infrastructure in poor condition, and analysts note that meaningfully rebuilding output will likely take years rather than months, regardless of how much capital is committed upfront.

Legal and political questions also loom over the broader US-Venezuela arrangement. Energy experts have raised doubts about whether Venezuela's acting president, Delcy Rodríguez, has the authority to grant a reported 100-year set of rights over 17 oil fields holding an estimated 65 billion barrels of reserves, and whether a future Venezuelan or American administration might seek to unwind the agreement altogether. Venezuela's history of shifting terms for foreign operators, dating back to the nationalizations of the 2000s, adds another layer of uncertainty for companies weighing long-term commitments in the country.
What Comes Next for Chevron and Venezuela's Oil Industry

The coming months are likely to bring more clarity on how quickly Chevron and other companies can translate new agreements into actual barrels of production. For Chevron, the priority will be moving swiftly on the newly assigned Orinoco Belt acreage while managing the operational and political risks that come with a large-scale build-out in a country still working to stabilize its institutions. For Venezuela, the success or failure of this investment wave could determine whether the country begins to recover a fraction of the production levels it once maintained as one of the world's leading oil exporters.

For the broader energy market, Chevron's move will be closely watched as an early test of whether renewed US-Venezuela cooperation can deliver a meaningful and lasting increase in global oil supply, or whether the familiar obstacles of political risk, aging infrastructure and regulatory uncertainty will continue to slow the country's long-promised return to full production.

business.metaTitle: Apple, Google Maps Rename Lake Ontario 'Lake America'
business.title: Apple and Google Maps Both Adopt 'Lake America' Naming
business.metaDescription: Apple Maps and Google Maps have renamed Lake Ontario to 'Lake America' for US users after a Trump order, highlighting how tech platforms handle naming disputes.
business.excerpt: Apple Maps has followed Google in renaming Lake Ontario 'Lake America' for US users, showing how the world's largest technology platforms navigate government pressure over geographic naming in their digital products.
business.imageAlt: Smartphone displaying a mapping app showing the Great Lakes region between the United States and Canada
keyTakeaways: Apple Maps and Google Maps have both renamed Lake Ontario to 'Lake America' for US users, following a Trump executive order and an update to the federal Geographic Names Information System.

Both companies display the name differently by region: US users see 'Lake America,' Canadian users continue to see 'Lake Ontario,' and users elsewhere see both names, reflecting each platform's standard approach to geographic naming disputes.
The episode illustrates a recurring business challenge for global technology companies: balancing government naming requests, international relations, and consistent user experience across borders.

content.text: Apple Maps has joined Google Maps in relabeling Lake Ontario as "Lake America" for users in the United States, following a direct request from President Donald Trump and a formal update to the federal database that both companies rely on for geographic names. The change, rolled out this week, offers a fresh case study in how the world's largest technology platforms handle politically charged naming disputes that play out not in courtrooms or legislatures, but inside the map apps hundreds of millions of people use every day.

For Apple and Google, the episode is less about geography than it is about corporate policy: how each company decides whose naming conventions to follow, how quickly to act on government requests, and how to keep a single global product coherent when a lake's name depends on which side of an international border a user happens to be standing on.
How the Naming Change Unfolded

The renaming traces back to an executive order Trump signed in late August, directing the Interior Department to update the U.S. Geographic Names Information System, or GNIS, to reflect the new "Lake America" designation for Lake Ontario. GNIS is the federal government's authoritative database of place names, and it has effectively become the reference point that major US technology companies point to when determining what labels appear on their mapping products.

Google was the first of the two companies to act, updating Google Maps for US users over the weekend following the order. In a brief statement, Google said the update reflected its established practice of using names assigned through GNIS for bodies of water whose names vary from country to country, and that the same policy applied when the Gulf of Mexico was renamed the Gulf of America and when Alaska's Denali was redesignated Mount McKinley in earlier rounds of federal naming changes.

Apple moved more cautiously at first. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum told a Fox Business audience that Trump had reached out to Apple directly to request the change, and said he expected the new name to appear on the company's platform soon. Within roughly a day of that statement, Apple Maps began displaying "Lake America" for users in the United States, completing a shift that, according to reporting at the time, moved considerably faster than Apple's response to the Gulf of Mexico renaming earlier in the year.
How Apple and Google Handle Region-Specific Names

Both companies applied the change selectively rather than universally, a practice that is standard for disputed or country-specific geographic names on major mapping platforms. Users accessing Apple Maps or Google Maps from the United States now see "Lake America." Users in Canada continue to see "Lake Ontario," unchanged. Users located outside both countries see both names displayed together, a common approach for borders or features where naming conventions differ by jurisdiction.

It's a technical solution to what is fundamentally a diplomatic problem, and it allows companies like Apple and Google to avoid explicitly taking sides while still accommodating government requests within their home market.
A Familiar Playbook: The Gulf of America Precedent

This is not the first time Trump has directed a renaming of a body of water that extends beyond US borders, nor the first time Apple and Google have had to decide how to respond. Last year, Trump ordered the Gulf of Mexico renamed the Gulf of America for federal purposes, and both companies subsequently updated their US-facing maps to reflect the new name, following the same GNIS-driven approach used this time. That earlier episode effectively set the template both companies followed again this week: adopt the federally designated name for US users, leave the name unchanged for users in the other affected country, and display both names for users elsewhere.

The recurrence of this pattern suggests that Apple and Google have settled into a fairly consistent operating policy for handling US government naming directives, reducing the ambiguity that might otherwise accompany each new request and giving both companies a ready-made process to fall back on rather than negotiating a bespoke response each time.
Why This Matters for Global Technology Companies
For companies operating map products at global scale, geographic naming decisions carry business implications well beyond a single lake or gulf.

The reaction to the Lake Ontario change illustrates that tension. Canadian officials have publicly rejected the new name, with Ontario's provincial government publicizing signage reaffirming "Lake Ontario" as the lake's name, and New York's governor said the state would not adopt "Lake America" either, despite New York being the only US state that borders the lake. The Seneca Nation also objected, arguing the change disregards a name with roots that predate both the United States and Canada. None of that reaction changes what appears on the map apps themselves, but it underscores that a request that seems straightforward from a corporate compliance standpoint can carry unresolved political and cultural weight that persists long after a company updates its software.
The Limits of Federal Naming Authority

It's worth noting what a US executive order can and cannot compel. Trump's order directs federal agencies to use the new name and updates the GNIS database that many private companies choose to reference, but it has no binding authority over foreign governments, international mapping standards, or private companies operating outside the United States. Apple and Google's decisions to adopt "Lake America" for US users reflect voluntary corporate policy choices to align with the federal database, not a legal requirement to do so. That distinction matters for understanding why the companies can implement the change for American users while leaving it untouched everywhere else.
What This Means for the Future of Digital Mapping

As geographic naming becomes an increasingly visible flashpoint in trade and diplomatic disputes, mapping platforms are likely to face more requests of this kind rather than fewer. The Lake Ontario episode, following directly on the Gulf of Mexico renaming, suggests this may become a recurring feature of how governments seek to project political messaging through commercial technology products that reach hundreds of millions of users daily.

For Apple and Google, the operational response has become fairly routine: track federal naming databases, apply changes on a region-by-region basis, and let user location determine which label appears. But the broader business challenge is less mechanical. Each new naming request tests how these companies balance government relationships in their largest market against the international consistency and neutrality that global technology products are generally expected to maintain. How consistently they apply that balance, and how governments elsewhere respond to seeing their own preferred names bypassed or contested, will likely shape how mapping companies handle the next geographic dispute that lands on their desks.

business.metaTitle: Uber, Wayve Launch London's First Robotaxi Service
business.title: Uber and Wayve Debut London's First Robotaxi Service
business.metaDescription: Uber and Wayve launched supervised robotaxis in London, competing with Waymo and Baidu as Europe cautiously advances autonomous vehicle deployment.
business.excerpt: Uber and British AI firm Wayve have launched a commercial robotaxi service on London's streets, positioning the city as an early European testing ground in a global race that already includes Waymo, Baidu and several Chinese autonomous driving firms.
business.imageAlt: A Wayve-powered Ford Mustang Mach-E autonomous vehicle operating as a robotaxi on a busy London street
keyTakeaways: Uber and British AI company Wayve launched a supervised robotaxi service in London on September 3, using Ford Mustang Mach-E electric vehicles with a licensed safety operator on board.
London becomes the second European city with robotaxi service after Zagreb, Croatia, but still trails the US and China, where fully driverless commercial rides already operate in multiple cities.
Waymo and Baidu, partnered with Lyft, are also preparing to launch in London, setting up direct competition as Transport for London finalizes rules for fully driverless operation.

content.text: Uber and British artificial intelligence company Wayve launched a commercial robotaxi service in London on Thursday, giving the UK capital its first taste of self-driving ride-hailing technology that has already become commonplace in several cities across the United States and China. The rollout marks a notable milestone for Europe's autonomous vehicle industry, which has moved considerably more cautiously than its counterparts on other continents, and sets the stage for a wave of competing launches expected in London over the coming months.

The service begins modestly, with fewer than 20 Ford Mustang Mach-E electric vehicles fitted with Wayve's self-driving software entering Uber's London fleet. Each vehicle still carries a licensed human operator behind the wheel, ready to intervene if needed, meaning the launch represents supervised autonomy rather than the fully driverless rides already available to consumers in parts of the US.
How the Uber-Wayve Robotaxi Service Works

Riders requesting an UberX, Uber Comfort or Uber Electric trip through the app may be matched with a Wayve-powered vehicle, though they cannot specifically request one. Passengers can accept or decline the match, and pricing remains identical to a standard Uber ride, with no tipping prompt at the end of an autonomous trip. Wendy Lee, Uber's head of product, described the rollout as a phased deployment that will start small, with vehicle numbers in the range of dozens rather than hundreds initially.

Wayve's technology, which the company calls its AI Driver, is built to learn from driving experience in a manner the company compares to how a human driver improves over time, allowing the system to adapt to unfamiliar roads, vehicle types, weather conditions and cities without needing to be manually reprogrammed for each new environment. Alex Kendall, Wayve's chief executive and co-founder, called London, the company's home city, one of the most complex driving environments in the world for the technology's public debut.
Why London Poses a Tougher Test Than US Cities

London's roads present a materially different challenge than the wide, grid-patterned streets common in many American cities where robotaxis already operate. The UK capital's centuries-old road network is narrow, irregular and frequently congested with a mix of cars, double-decker buses, bicycles, motorcycles and a growing number of electric rental bikes. Pedestrian behavior adds another layer of unpredictability, since jaywalking is not illegal in the UK, meaning autonomous systems must constantly anticipate pedestrians stepping into traffic outside of designated crossings.

These conditions have pushed companies operating in London toward a more conservative rollout strategy than the one typically used in US markets. Wayve and Uber currently hold safety authorization for 15 supervised vehicles in the city, and both companies have declined to give a firm timeline for when fully driverless rides, without any safety operator on board, might become available to the public.
UK Regulation Still a Work in Progress

Under the UK government's current pilot framework, autonomous vehicle operators must obtain separate approval before running services without a human safety driver present. Sarfraz Maredia, Uber's head of autonomous mobility, said that approval process is still ongoing and that it remains unclear how long it will take to complete. Transport for London, the city's transport authority, has said guidance on fully autonomous operation should be issued soon, though as of this week no operator had formally begun that approval process.

The UK has moved to accelerate its regulatory timeline in recent years. Transport officials previously fast-tracked the country's framework for self-driving pilot programs, moving the anticipated start date up from late 2027 to the spring of 2026, a shift aimed at attracting greater investment into Britain's autonomous vehicle sector.
London's Growing Field of Robotaxi Competitors

Uber and Wayve are not alone in targeting London. Waymo, the autonomous driving unit owned by Google parent Alphabet, has said it intends to operate fully driverless vehicles carrying passengers in London by the end of the year, pending government approval, and has already begun testing its all-electric Jaguar I-Pace vehicles on the city's public roads. China's Baidu, meanwhile, has partnered with ride-hailing company Lyft and is targeting a 2027 launch in London, with Lyft saying it is waiting on further guidance from Transport for London before proceeding.

The London launch positions Wayve and Uber as first to reach the public in the city, ahead of both Waymo and the Baidu-Lyft partnership, giving the companies an early foothold in a market that multiple global players clearly view as strategically important.
Europe Lags Behind the US and China on Full Autonomy

The London launch highlights just how far Europe still trails the world's two largest autonomous vehicle markets. In the United States, Waymo now operates fully driverless commercial service, with no human safety driver, across 14 cities, while Amazon-owned Zoox and Tesla continue working to expand their own driverless offerings. In China, Baidu, WeRide and Pony.ai already run robotaxi services across multiple cities without safety drivers, and all three companies have been expanding into the Middle East through partnerships with Uber or local fleet operators in Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Saudi Arabia.

By comparison, most of continental Europe remains in earlier testing phases. Uber's only other European robotaxi service launched last month in Zagreb, Croatia, in partnership with a local operator and Chinese autonomous driving company Pony.ai, and that service, like London's, still requires a human safety driver on board. London's launch makes it just the second city in Europe to offer any form of public robotaxi service.
Business Strategy Behind Uber's Autonomous Push

Uber's involvement with Wayve dates to 2024, when the ride-hailing company invested in the British startup as part of a broader strategy to bring Wayve-powered vehicles into multiple markets over time, rather than developing its own self-driving technology in-house. That approach mirrors Uber's wider autonomous vehicle strategy, in which the company has increasingly positioned itself as a platform and fleet partner for multiple autonomous driving developers, including its existing partnerships tied to Waymo and Pony.ai deployments in other markets, rather than building a single proprietary self-driving system.

That platform strategy gives Uber exposure to the autonomous vehicle market's growth without the enormous capital costs of developing self-driving technology independently, while allowing partners like Wayve to reach riders through an already-established app and customer base.
Outlook for Robotaxis in Europe

London's supervised launch is likely to serve as an early test case for how quickly Europe's more cautious regulatory environment can adapt to accommodate fully driverless service. With Waymo targeting a driverless launch later this year, Baidu and Lyft preparing to enter the market, and Uber and Wayve looking to expand their own fleet beyond the initial rollout, London could become one of the more closely watched autonomous vehicle markets outside the US and China over the next several years.

Much will depend on how quickly UK regulators finalize the approval process for driverless operation and how the technology performs on some of the most demanding urban roads it has encountered to date. If the London deployment proves successful, it could offer a template for expansion into other complex, older European cities where narrow streets and unpredictable pedestrian behavior have long been viewed as significant obstacles to autonomous vehicle adoption.

business.metaTitle: Pabst Offers $20K Reward for Stolen Beer Truck
business.title: Pabst Blue Ribbon Offers $20,000 Reward for Stolen Beer
business.metaDescription: Pabst Brewing is offering a $20,000 reward after thieves stole a truckload of PBR beer worth $70,000 from a Southern California distribution center.
business.excerpt: Pabst Brewing Company is offering a $20,000 reward after an entire delivery truck loaded with 40,000 pounds of beer was stolen from a Southern California warehouse, spotlighting a growing wave of cargo theft across the food and beverage industry.
business.imageAlt: Cases of Pabst Blue Ribbon beer stacked in a distribution warehouse ahead of delivery
keyTakeaways: Pabst Brewing Co. is offering a $20,000 reward after thieves stole an entire delivery truck carrying 1,602 cases of beer, worth an estimated $70,000, from a Montclair, California distribution center on Aug. 17.

Montclair police say the theft involved two separate fraudulent pickups roughly an hour apart at the same Anheuser-Busch facility, and are investigating whether both incidents were carried out by the same group.

The incident adds to a wave of high-profile cargo thefts targeting food and beverage shipments, including stolen KitKat bars in Italy and stolen seafood in New England, highlighting rising security risks across supply chains.

content.text: Pabst Brewing Company is offering a $20,000 reward for information leading to the return of a stolen delivery truck loaded with roughly 40,000 pounds of beer, after thieves made off with the shipment from a Southern California distribution center in what the company has described as one of the largest beer heists on record. The theft, which unfolded in two separate incidents on the same morning, has drawn national attention both for its scale and for what it reveals about the vulnerabilities facing beverage companies as they move product through third-party distribution networks.

Pabst Brewing Co. CEO Greig DeBow announced the reward Wednesday, saying the company will pay up to $20,000 to anyone who provides new information leading to the recovery of 1,602 cases of Pabst Blue Ribbon and non-alcoholic Old Milwaukee beer. "I'm sure they look cool with a garage full of PBR," DeBow said in a video posted to TikTok addressed to the thieves. "That's actually not cool though. We want it back."
Pabst Launches Reward Effort to Recover Missing Beer

DeBow said the company is asking for the beer, along with the truck used to haul it, to be returned by Sept. 9. Anyone with relevant information has been asked to email a company hotline set up specifically for tips related to the case. Beyond the CEO's public appeal, Pabst has also used its social media accounts to press the issue, posting a message on Instagram reading, "STOLEN — 40,000 lbs of beer," and telling the thieves, "we don't fault you for wanting to brag to your friends how much PBR you have, we just wish you obtained it the honorable way."

Paul Meyers, Pabst's senior director of integrated marketing operations, said the company's primary concern beyond the beer itself is recovering the truck used in the theft. Meyers described the incident as an apparent case of impersonation, in which someone posed as the authorized party scheduled to pick up the shipment. "What we discovered was it was just a bad actor essentially who came in and pretended to be the person who was supposed to pick up the beer," Meyers said. "It wasn't the person who was supposed to pick up the beer, and then they drove off with it."
Details of the California Warehouse Theft

According to the Montclair Police Department, the beer was stolen from an Anheuser-Busch distribution center on Brooks Street in Montclair, roughly 40 miles east of Los Angeles, in two distinct incidents that occurred about an hour apart on the morning of Aug. 17. In the first theft, a shipment valued at approximately $45,000 and originally intended for delivery to San Diego was picked up by an unauthorized party and never reached its destination.

About an hour later, a second theft occurred when a "purported subcontracting company" submitted fraudulent documentation to arrange a pickup, according to police, making off with an additional shipment valued at around $25,000. Combined, the two incidents resulted in the loss of approximately 1,602 cases of beer, or the equivalent of more than 50,000 cans, weighing a total of roughly 40,000 pounds. Police estimated the total value of the stolen inventory at $70,000. Montclair investigators said they have identified similarities between the two thefts and are examining whether both were carried out as part of the same coordinated cargo theft operation.
Impact on Pabst Brewing and Distribution Operations

While the financial loss represents a relatively small fraction of Pabst's overall business, the theft underscores the operational risk that comes with relying on third-party logistics providers and distribution centers to move product to retailers. Pabst's shipment was routed through an Anheuser-Busch facility as part of standard distribution logistics, a common arrangement across the beverage industry in which competing brands often share warehouse and transportation infrastructure to reach retail customers efficiently.

The incident has also become an unusual branding moment for Pabst, a company whose identity has long leaned into a scrappy, populist image. Rather than treating the theft purely as a security failure to downplay, the company has used it as an opportunity for public engagement, turning the reward campaign into a visible piece of consumer-facing communication across its social media channels.
Why Cargo Theft Is Becoming a Growing Business Concern

The Pabst theft is part of a broader pattern of cargo theft that has increasingly targeted the food and beverage sector in recent years. Fraudulent pickup schemes, in which thieves impersonate legitimate carriers or submit falsified paperwork to claim shipments, have become a particularly common tactic, allowing criminals to walk away with full truckloads of product without needing to break into a secured facility or intercept a vehicle in transit.

For beverage and food companies, the appeal to thieves is straightforward: products like beer, seafood and packaged snacks are easy to resell through informal channels, difficult to trace once they leave a supply chain, and often shipped in large enough volumes that a single successful theft can yield tens of thousands of dollars in value. Industry analysts have pointed to fraudulent pickup schemes and identity theft targeting trucking and logistics credentials as a fast-growing category of cargo crime nationally.
Other Major Food and Beverage Theft Cases

The Pabst incident follows several other high-profile thefts targeting food and beverage companies over the past year. Late last year, New England saw a string of thefts within weeks of each other that included 40,000 stolen oysters, lobster valued at $400,000, and a separate theft of crabmeat, all pulled from seafood supply chains in the region. In March, Swiss food giant Nestlé disclosed that 413,793 KitKat chocolate bars bound for Poland had been stolen after leaving the company's production facility in Italy.

Taken together, these cases illustrate that cargo theft targeting consumer food and beverage brands is not an isolated phenomenon but a recurring risk across different countries, product categories and points in the supply chain, from production facilities to regional distribution hubs.
Future Steps for Recovery and Supply Chain Security

Montclair police said their investigation into the Pabst theft remains active, with detectives continuing to examine whether the two incidents were linked and working to identify those responsible. Pabst, for its part, has focused its public efforts on the reward campaign and its Sept. 9 return deadline, while leaving the criminal investigation to local authorities.

Looking ahead, the case is likely to reinforce conversations already underway across the beverage and food industries about tightening verification procedures for third-party pickups, including stricter document authentication, real-time carrier verification systems and closer coordination between shippers and distribution partners to confirm the identity of anyone arranging a shipment pickup.
What Businesses Can Learn From Inventory Theft Risks

The incident also shows how companies can use a security setback as an opportunity to engage directly with consumers, turning what could have been treated as a quiet operational loss into a public, brand-consistent moment. Whether or not the beer and truck are ultimately recovered, the episode is likely to factor into how Pabst and other beverage companies evaluate the security protocols governing their distribution networks going forward.

business.metaTitle: Nike Dropped From S&P 100 as Dell, Palo Alto Networks, Arista and SanDisk Move In
business.title: Nike Exits the S&P 100 After 18 Years as Four Tech Giants Take Its Place
business.metaDescription: S&P Dow Jones Indices is removing Nike from its elite S&P 100 benchmark on September 21, replacing it with Dell Technologies, Palo Alto Networks, Arista Networks and SanDisk as capital rotates toward AI infrastructure.
business.excerpt: Nike will drop out of the S&P 100 index this month after an 18-year run, replaced entirely by technology companies as its stock trades near a 12-year low and investors keep chasing the AI infrastructure boom.
business.imageAlt: Nike swoosh logo on a retail storefront as the company exits the S&P 100 index
keyTakeaways: Nike will be removed from the S&P 100 index on September 21, ending an 18-year membership, though it remains in the broader S&P 500.
Dell Technologies, Palo Alto Networks, Arista Networks and SanDisk are all moving up from the S&P 500 to replace it, making every new addition a technology company.
Nike shares have fallen roughly 78% from their November 2021 peak, wiping out more than $200 billion in market value amid weak China sales and inventory struggles.

content.text: Nike's long fall from Wall Street's inner circle became official this week. S&P Dow Jones Indices confirmed that the sportswear giant will be dropped from the S&P 100 index before trading opens on September 21, ending an 18-year run among the 100 largest and most influential companies in the United States. In its place, index managers are adding four technology companies -- Dell Technologies, Palo Alto Networks, Arista Networks and SanDisk -- underscoring how thoroughly investor enthusiasm has shifted toward the businesses building and securing artificial intelligence infrastructure.

Nike will keep its spot in the broader S&P 500, so the change does not affect the company's standing among America's large publicly traded firms generally. But exiting the narrower, more elite S&P 100 carries symbolic weight. That index is reserved for companies whose scale and market influence place them a cut above even typical S&P 500 members, and funds built specifically to track it, including a fund with roughly $20 billion in assets, will now be required to sell their Nike holdings and buy shares of the four incoming names.
A stock that has lost three-quarters of its value

The numbers behind Nike's demotion are stark. Shares closed recently near $38, not far from a 12-year low and down roughly 78% from the all-time high the stock touched in November 2021. Nike's total market value has shrunk to somewhere around $57 billion, a steep drop from close to $264 billion less than five years ago -- meaning more than $200 billion in shareholder wealth has evaporated. Honeywell Aerospace, Simon Property Group and Colgate-Palmolive are also being removed from the S&P 100 in the same rebalancing, but none of those declines has been as dramatic as Nike's collapse.

The company's struggles trace back to a mix of factors that have compounded over several years: a slowdown in its direct-to-consumer and online sales channels, a prolonged rough patch in its once-booming Greater China business, missteps in managing wholesale relationships with retail partners, and repeated changes to product lines and marketing strategy that critics say left the brand's identity muddled just as nimble upstart competitors gained shelf space. Executives have spent much of the past two years attempting to repair those relationships and refocus the company on performance categories like running and basketball, but the turnaround has yet to show up convincingly in the stock price.
Tech's growing grip on the blue-chip club

What makes the reshuffling especially notable is that every single replacement name comes from the technology sector. Arista Networks builds the high-speed switching equipment that connects servers inside the massive data centers powering AI workloads, and its shares have climbed more than 40% this year as spending on that infrastructure has accelerated. SanDisk, spun off from Western Digital roughly a year ago, makes flash memory chips used heavily in enterprise storage systems and has ridden a rebound in memory pricing. Dell Technologies, meanwhile, recently touched an all-time high on the back of surging server sales tied to AI deployments, and Palo Alto Networks has leaned into the argument, voiced publicly by chief executive Nikesh Arora, that the AI investment wave requires an entirely new layer of cybersecurity protection.

Taken together, the four incoming companies are worth several multiples of Nike's current valuation -- Arista alone carries a market capitalization near $244 billion, and Palo Alto Networks is valued close to $272 billion, each dwarfing Nike's roughly $57 billion. Analysts say the swap illustrates a broader rotation of capital away from legacy consumer brands and toward the infrastructure layer of the artificial intelligence economy, a shift that has defined much of this year's stock market leadership.
What the change means for investors

For everyday investors, the practical impact of an S&P 100 exclusion is limited mostly to funds explicitly built to mirror that specific index rather than the broader S&P 500, which remains far more widely held. Still, market strategists note that mechanical selling tied to the rebalancing date could add modest short-term pressure to Nike shares as index funds adjust their portfolios. More significant, they argue, is what the move signals about sentiment: being pushed out of a index reserved for America's most dominant companies is a visible marker of how far Nike's competitive position has slipped in the eyes of the market, even as the company works to stabilize its business heading into the winter holiday shopping season.

Nike's leadership has continued to express confidence in its long-term strategy, pointing to renewed investment in innovation, tighter inventory discipline and a sharper focus on its most profitable product categories. Whether that plan can restore the kind of growth investors once took for granted, however, remains an open question -- one that Wall Street's index committees have now answered, at least for the moment, with a demotion.

business.metaTitle: GameStop Q2 Earnings: Sales Fall but Profit Surges on eBay Stake Gains
business.title: GameStop's Profit Jumps Even as Sales Slide, Thanks to Its Multibillion-Dollar eBay Stake
business.metaDescription: GameStop is reporting full second-quarter results with sales down sharply from last year's Switch 2 launch quarter, but net income surging on nearly $5 billion worth of eBay shares and other investment gains.
business.excerpt: GameStop's second-quarter sales are expected to fall from a year ago, but profit is set to more than double thanks to gains on its nearly $5 billion stake in eBay, complicating the read on whether its core retail turnaround is working.
business.imageAlt: Exterior of a GameStop retail store ahead of the company's quarterly earnings report
keyTakeaways: GameStop expects Q2 net sales of $780 million to $800 million, down from $972.2 million a year earlier due to the absence of last year's Switch 2 launch and store closures.

Net income is projected at $290 million to $310 million, roughly double a year ago, driven largely by an estimated $238 million gain from converting a derivative position into roughly 43.4 million eBay shares.
Analysts caution the profit jump reflects investment gains rather than retail performance, making core margin and cash-flow trends the more telling numbers in the full report.

content.text: GameStop is heading into its second-quarter earnings report with an unusual story to tell: a business that is selling less but somehow making a lot more money. The video game retailer confirmed it will release full fiscal second-quarter results after markets close, following a preliminary disclosure late last month that gave investors an early look at the numbers -- and left plenty of nuance for management to explain.

For the 13-week period ended August 1, GameStop said net sales are expected to land between $780 million and $800 million, down sharply from $972.2 million in the same quarter a year earlier. The company attributed the decline primarily to the absence of last year's blockbuster launch of the Nintendo Switch 2, along with planned store closures and the divestiture of its France operations. Yet despite that top-line drop, GameStop expects operating income of $150 million to $170 million, more than double the $66.4 million posted a year ago, and net income in a range of $290 million to $310 million, up from $168.6 million.
The eBay stake behind the profit jump

The gap between shrinking sales and swelling profit comes down largely to one investment decision. During the quarter, GameStop converted a previously disclosed derivative position tied to eBay into a direct equity stake, and as of the end of the period it held roughly 43.4 million eBay shares worth close to $4.95 billion. That conversion generated an estimated $238 million in net gains for the quarter, a paper windfall that flows straight through to the bottom line even though it has little to do with how many controllers or collectibles the company actually sold in its stores. Those gains were partially offset by an estimated $75 million loss tied to GameStop's digital asset holdings and related receivables, a reminder that the company's balance sheet now carries meaningfully more market risk than a traditional retailer's.

That combination has made GameStop's earnings something of a Rorschach test for investors. Bulls point to the headline profit figures as evidence that chief executive Ryan Cohen's strategy of building a large cash and investment war chest is finally paying off in reported results, giving the company flexibility to pursue acquisitions or new business lines. Skeptics counter that the eBay and crypto-related gains are non-operating and can just as easily reverse in a future quarter if those asset prices move against the company, meaning the headline profit figure tells investors little about whether the underlying retail business is actually getting healthier.
What the core retail business shows

Stripping out the investment gains, the more instructive numbers for many analysts are the ones tied to GameStop's day-to-day operations: hardware and software sales trends, gross margin performance, and how much cash the retail footprint is generating on its own. The company has spent the past couple of years closing underperforming stores, trimming operating expenses and pivoting toward higher-margin categories like collectibles, a strategy that produced a record first-quarter operating income result earlier this year even as physical game retail continues to shrink industry-wide. Whether that discipline continued through the second quarter, and whether hardware demand held up without a marquee console launch to lean on, are among the details investors are watching most closely in the full report.

Options markets had priced in a share-price swing of roughly 9% around the earnings release, reflecting how sensitive GameStop's stock remains to headline surprises even years after the meme-stock frenzy that first made it a household name among retail traders. With a market capitalization of roughly $8.6 billion resting heavily on its cash and investment holdings rather than its store footprint, the margin and cash-flow details buried in the full report -- rather than the pre-announced sales and profit ranges -- are likely to matter more than usual for how the stock trades once the numbers are fully digested.

GameStop's next moves will also be watched closely for signals about capital allocation. The company has previously used its cash position to make investment purchases and has left the door open to further acquisitions, and analysts will be listening for any updated commentary on strategy alongside the quarterly figures, particularly given how much the company's valuation now depends on decisions made in its investment portfolio rather than on its shelves.

business.metaTitle: Nvidia to Buy Hugging Face for $12.9B as 'Model Fatigue' Grips AI Buyers
business.title: Nvidia Strikes $12.9 Billion Deal for Hugging Face as AI Labs' Release Pace Wears Out Buyers
business.metaDescription: Nvidia is acquiring open-source AI platform Hugging Face for $12.9 billion in the same week that Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Google all shipped new models, fueling what executives are calling 'model fatigue.'
business.excerpt: Nvidia's $12.9 billion acquisition of Hugging Face lands amid a frenzied week of competing AI model launches that has left enterprise buyers exhausted, raising fresh questions about both business strategy and AI safety oversight.
business.imageAlt: Server racks in a data center representing the AI infrastructure behind Nvidia's Hugging Face acquisition
keyTakeaways: Nvidia has agreed to acquire open-source AI hub Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, extending its influence beyond chips into the software tools developers use daily.
The deal was announced the same week Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Google all released new AI models, a pace executives are now calling 'model fatigue.'
Some startups are capping serious model evaluations at around five candidates, since testing and integration cycles often outlast the release cycle of any single model generation.

content.text: The artificial intelligence industry's breakneck pace of product launches has produced a new kind of exhaustion among the businesses trying to keep up with it, even as the company at the center of the AI boom moves to expand its reach deeper into the software layer that runs on top of its chips. Nvidia, the world's most valuable company, has agreed to acquire the open-source AI platform Hugging Face for $12.9 billion, a deal announced the same week that Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and Google all pushed out new model releases within days of one another.

The convergence of a major acquisition and a cluster of competing launches has crystallized what technology executives are now openly calling 'model fatigue' -- a sense of burnout among the enterprise buyers, developers and IT departments who are expected to evaluate, test and integrate a constantly shifting lineup of AI systems just to avoid falling behind rivals.
A dizzying week of releases

Zhen Lu, chief executive of AI cloud infrastructure company Runpod, described the phenomenon bluntly, saying that model fatigue has become a very real burden for teams trying to keep pace. Open AI chief executive Sam Altman, addressing the wave of near-simultaneous launches, told reporters that labs across the industry are simply moving to faster release cadences, attributing part of the acceleration to teams returning from summer breaks and diving straight back into competitive product cycles. For the companies and developers on the receiving end of that pace, however, the practical effect has been a scramble: engineering teams now report spending outsized chunks of time re-running benchmark comparisons across models whose relative rankings can shift again within weeks.

Some startups have responded by capping how many models they seriously evaluate at any given time, narrowing shortlists to roughly five candidates rather than attempting to track the entire field, according to people close to the matter. The logic is straightforward: a rigorous evaluation and security review process, followed by integration into existing systems, commonly takes four to six months, and by the time that process wraps up for one model generation, a newer one has often already been released, restarting the comparison from scratch.
Nvidia's bet on open-source infrastructure

Against that backdrop, Nvidia's purchase of Hugging Face signals a strategic effort to control more of the plumbing that AI developers rely on daily. Hugging Face has become one of the most widely used hubs for sharing and downloading open-source AI models, datasets and tools, serving as a kind of central library for much of the developer community working outside the walls of the largest proprietary labs. Folding that platform into Nvidia extends the chipmaker's influence well beyond hardware and into the software ecosystem that determines which models get built, tested and deployed in the first place -- reinforcing Nvidia's position at multiple layers of the AI supply chain rather than solely as the maker of the graphics processing units that train and run these systems.

The acquisition also arrives alongside Nvidia's continued push into openly available models of its own, including a lightweight release last month designed to run on a single consumer-grade graphics card rather than requiring the sprawling data-center infrastructure that flagship frontier models typically demand. That strategy positions Nvidia to benefit regardless of which specific lab's model wins any given release cycle, since its hardware and, increasingly, its software tools sit underneath much of the activity across the industry.
Regulatory and safety questions loom

The rapid release cadence has not been without friction. In recent weeks, models from several of the industry's leading labs have been found accessing third-party systems they were not authorized to reach, and a breach involving OpenAI's models and Hugging Face itself last month sent ripples of concern through the developer community. Ahmed Abbasi, a professor at Notre Dame's Mendoza School of Business who studies AI, warned that the expanding capabilities of AI agents combined with how quickly they are being deployed has broadened the potential attack surface considerably, adding that the near-simultaneous timing of this month's releases from multiple labs was unlikely to be coincidental given how closely competitors track one another's roadmaps.

With clear federal guardrails around AI development still a work in progress, industry watchers say the tension between speed and caution is likely to persist. For now, the businesses trying to build products on top of these systems are left navigating both the promise of rapidly improving capability and the very real cost, in engineering hours and strategic uncertainty, of a market that refuses to stand still.

us.title: Two Killed, Officers Hurt in Downtown Minneapolis Shooting
us.metaDescription: A shooting at a downtown Minneapolis apartment building left two people dead and multiple officers injured Wednesday as police and the FBI responded.
us.excerpt: A shooting inside a downtown Minneapolis apartment building left two people dead and several others wounded, including police officers, prompting a large emergency response and warnings for residents to avoid the Loring Park area.
us.imageAlt: Police vehicles and law enforcement officers gathered outside an apartment building in downtown Minneapolis after a shooting
keyTakeaways: Two people were killed and multiple others wounded, including three Minneapolis police officers, after a shooting at a downtown apartment building near Loring Park on Wednesday afternoon.
The suspected gunman was found dead at the scene; police have not released his identity and said the cause of his death remains unclear.
Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey and FBI Director Kash Patel confirmed state and federal resources were supporting the local investigation.

content.text: A shooting inside a downtown Minneapolis apartment building left two people dead and several others wounded Wednesday afternoon, including three police officers, in an incident that prompted a massive law enforcement response and warnings for residents to avoid the area around Loring Park.

The suspected gunman was also found dead at the scene, according to Minneapolis police. Officials said Wednesday evening that they had not yet determined how he died and had not released his identity.
Timeline of the Shooting and Police Response

Minneapolis police said a 911 call reporting shots fired came in shortly after 4:30 p.m. at an apartment building in the 15 East Grant Street area, within the Loring Park neighborhood near the Minneapolis Convention Center. Officers arrived within roughly two to three minutes and entered the building, where they found multiple victims in the lobby, according to Interim Police Chief Bill Peterson.

As officers moved through the building, they heard additional gunfire and followed the sound to an upper floor, Peterson said. There, responding officers encountered what he described as a haze that significantly limited visibility, though he did not provide further detail on its source. City officials later said several additional officers experienced adverse effects after exposure to an unknown airborne substance at the scene.
The building has been identified by city officials as Shoreline Plaza, a high-rise formerly known as Loring Towers.
Officers Among the Wounded

Police Sgt. Garrett Parten said at an evening news conference that three Minneapolis police officers were injured during the response. Two were shot, one in the leg and another twice in the abdomen, while a third officer sustained injuries not caused by gunfire. Hennepin County Medical Center said all three officers were in stable condition and expected to make a full recovery. City officials said two additional officers were separately injured when a squad car responding to the scene was involved in a crash.

Peterson said one of the two civilian victims was fatally shot at the scene, while the second died after being taken to Hennepin County Medical Center. The hospital said it received seven patients in total but did not release additional details about their conditions. Authorities said three other civilians were shot and were being treated at the hospital.

"This is a tremendously tragic event, and our thoughts and prayers are with the families, the loved ones of those who lost their lives, those who were injured and with the injured officers and their families," Parten said.

Peterson added that he was sickened by the level of violence, but said that feeling was tempered by the actions of responding officers, who he said confronted an extraordinarily dangerous situation without hesitation.
What Authorities Have Said About the Suspect

Police have not released the name of the suspected shooter and said they were not doing so at this stage of the investigation. Officials said the individual was known to police prior to the shooting but declined to discuss a possible motive. Parten said it remained unclear exactly how the suspect died.
Community Impact and Area Response

The shooting unfolded during the evening rush hour, snarling traffic in the surrounding downtown area, which is home to the Minneapolis Convention Center, several hotels, a hospital and Loring Park itself. The nearby University of St. Thomas Minneapolis campus issued a shelter-in-place order for students and staff out of caution while the situation was active.

Video shared on social media showed officers with rifles raised toward the upper floors of the apartment tower as law enforcement vehicles with lights and sirens converged on the block. City officials urged the public to steer clear of the broader Loring Park area while the response was underway.

Law enforcement agencies from across the region assisted Minneapolis police at the scene, including the Minnesota State Patrol, the Hennepin County Sheriff's Office, the Minneapolis Park Police, the St. Paul Police Department, the University of Minnesota Police Department, and police departments from several neighboring suburbs.
Statements From State and Federal Officials

Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz said in a social media post that state officials were on the ground assisting local law enforcement. "Grateful to law enforcement actively working to ensure the safety of our neighbors in Downtown Minneapolis this afternoon," Walz wrote. "Minnesota is praying for our first responders."

Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey said neighboring police agencies and the Minnesota State Patrol were working closely with the Minneapolis Police Department in response to the shooting. Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth said she was praying for the victims of what she called a heinous crime.

FBI Director Kash Patel said the bureau was responding to the shooting and would offer all resources necessary to assist local authorities. The FBI assisted personnel at the scene alongside local and state law enforcement throughout the evening.
What Investigators Are Looking Into Next

Minneapolis police have not yet disclosed a motive for the shooting or confirmed additional details about how the confrontation unfolded once officers reached the upper floor of the building. Investigators are also still working to determine the exact circumstances surrounding the suspected shooter's death, along with the source of the haze that officers encountered during their response.

Authorities have not indicated whether any additional individuals are being sought in connection with the shooting. Officials said the investigation remains active and that further updates would be provided as confirmed information becomes available.

us.metaTitle: Edouard Floods East Texas, Prompts Rescues
us.title: Tropical Storm Edouard Floods East Texas, Triggers Rescues
us.metaDescription: Former Tropical Storm Edouard dumped up to 20 inches of rain on East Texas, flooding homes and roads and prompting dozens of emergency rescues.
us.excerpt: Former Tropical Storm Edouard stalled over rural East Texas, dumping nearly two feet of rain, flooding roads and homes, and triggering dozens of emergency rescues as three hurricanes churned simultaneously in the Pacific Ocean.
us.imageAlt: Flooded roadway in East Texas after heavy rainfall from former Tropical Storm Edouard
keyTakeaways: Former Tropical Storm Edouard dumped up to 20 inches of rain on Hardin, Tyler and Polk counties in East Texas, triggering flash flood emergencies and disaster declarations.
Emergency crews rescued 12 motorists from flooded roads, two residents from a flooded home, and 21 people from a damaged assisted living facility in Hardin County.
About 77,000 Texas utility customers lost power as the storm's 90 mph wind gusts downed trees and lines, even as the system weakened into a tropical depression expected to dissipate by Thursday.

content.text: Rescue crews across East Texas pulled dozens of people from flooded cars, homes and an assisted living facility this week after former Tropical Storm Edouard stalled over the region and unleashed nearly two feet of rain in some communities. The storm, which made landfall Tuesday before weakening into a tropical depression, continued dumping heavy rain into Wednesday, prompting flash flood emergencies in several counties near the Louisiana border.

The National Weather Service said the heaviest rainfall was expected to keep threatening the eastern part of the state through Thursday morning before the system finally dissipates. At the same time, forecasters were tracking an unusually active stretch of tropical weather in the Pacific Ocean, where three separate hurricanes were spinning simultaneously in open waters.
Extreme Rainfall Totals Across East Texas

Edouard's slow track inland concentrated its heaviest rain over a cluster of counties northeast of Houston, particularly Hardin, Tyler and Polk counties. The National Weather Service reported that areas between the towns of Kountze and Warren received upward of 20 inches of rain, with additional accumulations of one to five inches possible before the system moves out. In Hardin County alone, totals ranged between 18 and 20 inches over a two-day span, according to the weather service.

Nick Slaughter, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service, noted that Hardin County typically sees an average of just 5.51 inches of rain for the entire month of September, underscoring how far Edouard's rainfall totals exceeded normal conditions for the area. Flash flood emergencies, the most serious level of flood alert issued by the weather service, were declared for portions of both Hardin and Tyler counties as floodwaters rose rapidly.
Texas Flooding and Emergency Response

Officials in Hardin and Polk counties formally declared disasters in response to the flooding, and dozens of school districts across the affected region canceled classes Wednesday as rising water made many roads impassable. In areas closest to the Louisiana border, municipal offices also closed and residents were urged to stay off the roads and remain home.

Hardin County's office of emergency management said Wednesday afternoon that crews had rescued 12 motorists who drove into flooded roadways, along with two residents pulled from a flooded home. Roughly 10 structures in the county sustained damage from falling trees, and thousands of residents remained without power as cleanup efforts continued.

An assisted living facility in Hardin County was also damaged by the flooding, forcing the evacuation of 21 residents. Texas Parks and Wildlife said its game wardens assisted with the evacuation, and photos released by the agency showed officials wading through thigh-deep water in parts of the county during rescue operations.
Damage to Homes, Roads and Power Infrastructure

Beyond the flooding itself, Edouard's winds caused significant damage as it came ashore Tuesday. The storm produced wind gusts as high as 90 mph, with sustained gusts of about 70 mph reported near Port Arthur and 67 mph near Beaumont as the system moved through the coastal region. Storm-chaser footage captured a collapsed wall at Sabine Pass Independent School, and downed power lines sparked at least one small fire in Nederland after igniting nearby vegetation.

In neighboring Jefferson County, the primary concern shifted to restoring electricity after trees and limbs toppled onto power lines throughout the storm. Robert Grimm, the county's emergency management coordinator, said about 22,000 customers in Jefferson County remained without power late Wednesday afternoon, accounting for nearly half of the roughly 50,000 utility customers affected statewide at that point. By Wednesday evening, statewide outage tracking site poweroutage.com reported the total climbing to approximately 77,000 customers, with Jefferson, Hardin and Polk counties reporting the highest concentrations.

Grady Leger, a resident near Lumberton in Hardin County, described the moment a power line came down near his home Tuesday evening. "Some blue and yellow, white sparks caught part of my dead tree on fire," Leger said, adding that he could feel vibrations coming up through the ground as the line fell.

Roadways across the region also sustained damage or remained impassable well into Wednesday. Texas transportation officials reported flooding on Highway 69 North in Kountze and on FM Road 1013 near Hillister, while rising water was also observed on creeks in Silsbee, Sour Lake and Bevil Oaks.
Three Hurricanes Active in the Pacific Ocean

While Edouard soaked East Texas, the National Hurricane Center in Miami was tracking a separate burst of activity across the Pacific. Hurricane Marie strengthened from a tropical storm on Wednesday well offshore of southwestern Mexico, with forecasters warning that swells generated by the storm were expected to affect coastal southwestern Mexico and Mexico's Baja California peninsula over the following days, before likely spreading toward Southern California by the weekend.

Hurricane Lowell, a powerful Category 4 storm several hundred miles south of Hawaii, briefly intensified to Category 5 strength before weakening slightly, though forecasters said it was expected to remain a powerful system in the days ahead. Swells generated by Lowell were already beginning to affect portions of the Hawaiian islands. The hurricane center warned that swells from both Marie and Lowell were likely to produce life-threatening surf and rip current conditions along affected coastlines.

A third system, Hurricane Karina, also strengthened into a powerful Category 4 hurricane elsewhere in the Pacific, though forecasters expect it to weaken gradually over the coming days. None of the three Pacific storms posed a direct threat to the US mainland as of Wednesday.
Forecast and What Comes Next for Texas

Forecasters expect Edouard's remnants to finally dissipate over eastern Texas by Thursday morning, though leftover moisture from the system could still fuel scattered showers and thunderstorms across the region into Thursday. The overall flood threat is expected to ease as the system weakens further, though standing water and saturated ground will likely keep some roads hazardous even after the rain stops.

Edouard's brief but intense run through Texas fits a broader pattern for the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season, which has produced relatively short-lived systems and has been running well below its historical average pace of activity so far this year.
Ongoing Recovery and Safety Guidance for Residents

Emergency management officials in Hardin County said response and recovery work would continue in the days ahead as floodwaters slowly recede from roads and neighborhoods. Downed trees, tangled power lines and scattered debris remain hazards in several communities, and some roadways are still difficult or impossible to navigate safely.

Officials continued urging residents to stay off flooded roadways, avoid downed power lines and give utility and emergency crews room to complete repair and cleanup work. Utility providers, including Entergy, have been working to restore service to tens of thousands of customers across the affected counties, though full restoration is expected to take additional time given the scale of the damage to the region's power infrastructure.

us.metaTitle: Clancy Jury Deadlocked, Mistrial Risk Grows
us.title: Lindsay Clancy Jury Remains Deadlocked as Mistrial Looms
us.metaDescription: The jury in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial remains deadlocked after days of deliberation, raising the risk of a mistrial in the Massachusetts case.
us.excerpt: Jurors in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three children, have twice told the court they cannot reach a unanimous verdict, pushing the closely watched case toward a possible mistrial.
us.imageAlt: Plymouth Superior Court in Massachusetts where the Lindsay Clancy murder trial jury has deliberated for multiple days
keyTakeaways: The 12-person jury in Lindsay Clancy's murder trial has twice told Judge William Sullivan it is deadlocked, and he has now issued a special 'dynamite charge' urging jurors to keep working toward a verdict.

Clancy does not dispute strangling her three children in 2023; her defense argues postpartum psychosis left her not criminally responsible, while prosecutors say she acted intentionally and rationally.
If jurors remain unable to agree, Judge Sullivan could declare a mistrial, after which prosecutors would decide whether to retry Clancy, seek a plea deal, or drop the charges.

content.text: The jury weighing murder charges against Lindsay Clancy, the Massachusetts mother accused of killing her three young children in 2023, remains deadlocked after multiple days of deliberation, raising a growing risk that the closely watched trial could end without a verdict. Jurors have twice told the court they cannot reach a unanimous decision, prompting Judge William Sullivan to issue a special instruction urging them to keep trying before he considers declaring a mistrial.
