Clancy, 36, a former labor and delivery nurse, does not dispute that she strangled her children, Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months, with exercise resistance bands inside the family's Duxbury home in January 2023. The central legal question facing jurors is not whether she caused her children's deaths, but whether she was criminally responsible for her actions at the time, a distinction that has placed postpartum psychosis and the legal standard for criminal responsibility at the heart of the case.
A Deadlocked Jury and the Judge's Response

The 12-person jury, made up of nine women and three men, began deliberating in late August after roughly a month of testimony. By early September, after nearly 30 hours of deliberation spread across multiple days, jurors sent Judge Sullivan a note stating they were unable to reach a unanimous decision. Sullivan initially responded by directing them to continue deliberating, but when jurors reported the same impasse a second time, he read them what is formally known as the Tuey-Rodriguez instruction, sometimes referred to informally as a "dynamite charge."

That instruction asks jurors to reconsider the reasonableness of their own views and those of fellow jurors without abandoning their sincerely held convictions simply to reach agreement. Sullivan told jurors that no one could say a future jury would be more intelligent, impartial or capable of deciding the case than the one currently seated. Massachusetts courts generally treat the Tuey-Rodriguez charge as a final, formal push toward a verdict, and if jurors continue to report deadlock after receiving it, a judge may move to declare a mistrial.
The Evidence and Testimony Presented at Trial

Over the course of the trial, prosecutors called more than 70 witnesses, including members of Clancy's family, friends, first responders, investigators and medical providers, before resting their case in mid-August. The defense subsequently called ten witnesses of its own, including psychiatric experts who testified that Clancy was suffering from postpartum psychosis at the time of the killings. Prosecutors later presented a rebuttal case featuring three additional mental health experts who testified that Clancy was not psychotic when she killed her children.

Jurors also heard testimony describing the decline in Clancy's mental health in the months leading up to the killings, including details about medications she had been prescribed and a brief stay at a psychiatric hospital. The trial included roughly 300 exhibits for jurors to review, a volume defense attorney Kevin Reddington said outside the courthouse has required considerable effort from the panel. "They've been incredibly hard-working, paying attention through the whole trial," Reddington told reporters.
The Role of Postpartum Psychosis in the Defense

Clancy's defense has centered on the argument that she should not be held criminally responsible because she was in the grip of severe postpartum psychosis when she killed her children. Her attorneys have said she believed she heard a voice instructing her to kill the children so that she could then end her own life. After the killings, Clancy jumped from a second-floor window of the home in an apparent suicide attempt and remains paralyzed from the waist down.

Prosecutors have pushed back on that account, arguing that Clancy acted "intentionally, rationally and swiftly," and have questioned the seriousness of her suicide attempt. They have also argued that Clancy deliberately sent her then-husband, Patrick Clancy, out of the home on errands before carrying out the killings, which prosecutors say points to premeditation rather than a psychotic break.

Patrick Clancy testified as the trial's first witness after opening statements in late July. He has said in public interviews that he forgives his now ex-wife, describing her as someone who was ill rather than someone who acted out of malice.
What Happens if Jurors Cannot Reach a Verdict

If the jury remains unable to agree even after the Tuey-Rodriguez instruction, Judge Sullivan has the authority to declare a mistrial due to a hung jury. A mistrial would not resolve the underlying charges against Clancy, which would remain pending. Prosecutors would then need to decide whether to retry the case before an entirely new jury, attempt to negotiate a plea agreement with Clancy's defense team, or drop the charges altogether.

Legal analysts not involved in the case have noted that Massachusetts has seen deadlocked juries lead to mistrials in other high-profile cases in recent years, including the first murder trial of Karen Read in 2024, which ended in a hung jury before prosecutors retried the case; Read was ultimately acquitted following a 2025 retrial. Brad Bailey, a Boston defense attorney and former prosecutor who is not involved in the Clancy case, has said that while a retrial remains possible, Clancy's defense team is likely to push prosecutors toward dropping the charges rather than proceeding through another full trial.
Possible Verdicts if Jurors Reach a Decision

Should the jury ultimately reach a unanimous decision, several outcomes remain legally possible. Jurors could convict Clancy of first-degree murder, second-degree murder or manslaughter if they conclude she was criminally responsible for her children's deaths, with a murder conviction carrying the possibility of a life prison sentence. Alternatively, jurors could acquit Clancy if they find her mental state at the time meets the legal standard for lacking criminal responsibility. Even in the event of an acquittal, a judge could still order Clancy confined to a mental health facility if a subsequent evaluation determines she poses a danger to the public.
A Case That Has Drawn National Attention

The trial, which has been livestreamed and drawn packed courtrooms of reporters and spectators since jury selection began in July, has stirred broader public debate over maternal mental health after childbirth and how the criminal justice system should weigh severe postpartum psychiatric illness against personal culpability. The case has divided public opinion, with some viewing Clancy as a mother failed by inadequate mental health treatment and others focused on the loss of three young lives.
What Comes Next in the Court Process

For now, deliberations are set to continue, with jurors returning to the Plymouth Superior Court courtroom to resume their discussions. Judge Sullivan has thanked jurors repeatedly for their diligence and instructed them not to discuss, read about or research the case outside the courtroom. Whether the panel ultimately reaches a unanimous verdict or the judge is forced to declare a mistrial, the case is expected to remain a focal point of both legal and public attention given the questions it raises about mental illness, motherhood and criminal accountability under Massachusetts law.

us.metaTitle: Judge Blocks Trump's New Birthright Citizenship Order
us.title: Federal Judge Blocks Trump's Latest Birthright Citizenship Order
us.metaDescription: A federal judge blocked Trump's new executive order limiting birthright citizenship, citing Supreme Court precedent and the 14th Amendment.
us.excerpt: A federal judge in Maryland has blocked President Trump's newest attempt to narrow birthright citizenship, ruling the executive order is likely unconstitutional and citing a Supreme Court decision that struck down a similar effort earlier this year.
us.imageAlt: The United States Constitution with a gavel, representing a federal court ruling on birthright citizenship under the 14th Amendment
keyTakeaways: US District Judge Deborah Boardman issued a preliminary injunction blocking Trump's August 2026 executive order narrowing birthright citizenship, calling it 'almost certainly unconstitutional.'
The ruling cites the Supreme Court's June decision that struck down Trump's original 2025 birthright citizenship order, which sought to deny citizenship based on parents' immigration status.
The administration is expected to appeal the injunction, potentially setting up another Supreme Court review of the scope of the 14th Amendment's Citizenship Clause.

content.text: A federal judge in Maryland has blocked President Donald Trump's latest attempt to narrow birthright citizenship, ruling that his newest executive order is likely unconstitutional and directly conflicts with a Supreme Court decision issued just months earlier. US District Judge Deborah Boardman issued a preliminary injunction Wednesday against the order, which the administration had framed as an effort to curb so-called birth tourism and close what officials described as loopholes in citizenship law.

The ruling marks the second time in 2026 that a court has stopped Trump from implementing changes to birthright citizenship, a right guaranteed under the 14th Amendment since its ratification in 1868. It also intensifies a legal standoff between the White House and federal courts that has already reached the Supreme Court once this year and appears likely to return there.
What the Judge Ruled

In a 35-page opinion, Boardman wrote that Trump's August executive order limiting who qualifies for automatic citizenship at birth "is almost certainly unconstitutional," and granted a preliminary injunction preventing federal agencies from enforcing it while the underlying lawsuit proceeds. The injunction applies to a certified class of plaintiffs represented in the case and blocks the government from denying citizenship documents to children who fall within the categories targeted by the order.

"The Supreme Court has spoken: Children in the certified class are 'citizens at birth,'" Boardman wrote, directly invoking the high court's June ruling that struck down an earlier, broader version of Trump's birthright citizenship order. She added that the president has, since the start of his second term in January 2025, repeatedly used executive action to try to "upend our country's longstanding tradition of birthright citizenship" and narrow rights guaranteed under the Citizenship Clause.

Boardman, who was appointed to the federal bench by President Joe Biden, is not new to this litigation. She previously blocked an earlier version of Trump's birthright citizenship order in February 2025, issuing a nationwide injunction at that time after finding that no court in the country had ever endorsed the administration's interpretation of the 14th Amendment. In this latest ruling, she reiterated that position, writing that no court has sided with the administration's reading of the Constitution on this issue and that her court "will not be the first."
The Constitutional Foundation of Birthright Citizenship

Birthright citizenship traces back to the Citizenship Clause of the 14th Amendment, ratified in 1868 in the aftermath of the Civil War. Under longstanding legal interpretation, the amendment guarantees that virtually anyone born on US soil is automatically a citizen at birth, regardless of their parents' immigration status, with only narrow, historically recognized exceptions such as children born to foreign diplomats. That interpretation has governed US citizenship law and practice for more than 150 years.
What the August Executive Order Sought to Do

Trump's August order was a narrower follow-up to a more sweeping directive he signed on his first day back in office in January 2025, which had sought to deny citizenship to children born to parents who were in the country illegally or on a temporary basis. The Supreme Court struck down that original order in June, prompting the administration to draft a revised version targeting more specific categories of people.

The August order sought to deny automatic citizenship to children born to parents connected to foreign embassies or organizations, to anyone the administration classified as an "alien enemy," and to those the order described as engaging in "birth tourism," defined as entering the US on a nonimmigrant visa specifically to give birth on American soil. The order also targeted children born to adults who the government determined had "engaged in a commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship," a category that left some families concerned that ordinary actions, such as purchasing airfare to the US before becoming pregnant, could be used against them.
Arguments From the Families and Advocacy Groups

The lawsuit was brought by a group of immigrant families along with three advocacy organizations: We Are CASA, the Asylum Seeker Advocacy Project, and the Institute for Constitutional Advocacy and Protection. The plaintiffs argued that the executive branch had applied an overly broad and inconsistent standard for determining who counts as an "alien enemy," at times relying on speculation or unverified information rather than clear evidence.

Some families told the court they feared their children could lose access to citizenship simply because a distant relative had a tangential connection to a gang in their home country, even though the parents themselves had no such ties. Attorneys for the plaintiffs said the resulting uncertainty left affected families in a state of confusion and fear about their children's legal status.

Shana Khader, legal director at We Are CASA, said in a statement following the ruling that the administration would not succeed in its efforts. "The White House must recognize it will not succeed in stripping children of their right to citizenship, evading binding court decisions or placing the president's anti-immigrant agenda above the Constitution," Khader said.
The Administration's Position

Government attorneys had argued that the request to block the order was premature, contending that the federal agencies responsible for enforcing it would rely on "appropriate measures" and official guidance that had not yet been issued. Boardman rejected that argument directly, writing that regardless of what future guidance might say, the order itself "commands agencies to deny citizenship documents to several broad categories of children," meaning the harm to affected families was not speculative.

The judge also wrote separately that the government could not claim a legitimate interest in enforcing an order she considers likely unconstitutional, and that the narrow carve-outs described in the August order bear little resemblance to the limited historical exceptions to birthright citizenship that the Supreme Court has previously recognized. The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the ruling.
Previous Legal Battles Over Birthright Citizenship

This is not the first time federal courts have intervened to stop changes to birthright citizenship under the current administration. Trump's original January 2025 order was blocked by multiple federal judges within weeks of its signing, including a ruling from Seattle-based Judge John Coughenour, who at the time described the order as "blatantly unconstitutional" and said in more than four decades on the bench he could not recall a case so clearly at odds with the Constitution. Boardman's own nationwide injunction against that earlier order followed shortly after, setting the stage for the case's eventual path to the Supreme Court, which ruled against the administration in June.
What Happens Next in the Legal Process

Wednesday's ruling is a preliminary injunction, meaning it blocks enforcement of the August order while the underlying class-action lawsuit continues, rather than issuing a final, permanent resolution of the case. The administration is widely expected to appeal the decision, a move that could send the dispute to the US Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit and, potentially, back to the Supreme Court for further review of how far a president's executive authority extends over the scope of the Citizenship Clause.
Broader Implications for Immigration Law and Presidential Authority

The repeated legal setbacks underscore a broader constitutional question that has repeatedly resurfaced throughout Trump's second term: whether a president can use executive orders to reshape citizenship rules that have traditionally been understood as fixed by constitutional text and longstanding Supreme Court precedent. Wednesday's decision suggests that, for now, federal courts continue to view birthright citizenship as settled constitutional law rather than a policy question open to reinterpretation through executive action, even as the administration continues to test that boundary through successive, narrower versions of its original order.

us.metaTitle: Whistleblower warns USPS mail-ballot system could disrupt the midterms
us.title: Whistleblower warns USPS mail-ballot system could disrupt the midterms
us.metaDescription: A federal official's disclosure alleges the Postal Service's rushed new ballot-verification system could prevent millions of Americans from receiving their mail ballots on time.
us.excerpt: A federal official's disclosure alleges the Postal Service's rushed new ballot-verification system could prevent millions of Americans from receiving their mail ballots on time.
us.imageAlt: Mail ballots being sorted, illustrating concerns over the USPS mail-voting system
keyTakeaways: A whistleblower says the new USPS ballot portal is untested and rushed
A single failed barcode scan could reject an entire batch of 10,000 ballots
Key parts of the underlying executive order remain blocked in federal court

content.text: A federal whistleblower has warned that a new Postal Service system for processing mail ballots is so rushed and untested that it risks disrupting the upcoming midterm elections, according to a disclosure made public this week. The anonymous official, whose account was provided to Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut through the nonprofit group Whistleblower Aid, raised what the disclosure describes as grave concerns that the Trump administration has downplayed the likelihood of major failures in ballot delivery.

At the center of the complaint is a new Postal Service IT system, described internally as a portal, that is meant to verify mail ballots against a federal database before they reach voters. According to the whistleblower, the system's design creates an unusually high risk of mass failure: if even a single barcode among a batch of 10,000 ballots fails to scan correctly during verification, the entire batch could be rejected and sent back to the state that issued it, potentially stranding thousands of voters without ballots just as the midterm voting window opens.
A system built under legal pressure

The portal stems from an executive order signed by President Trump earlier this year directing federal agencies to tighten verification requirements for mail-in voting, part of a broader push the administration has framed as an effort to curb illegal voting by non-citizens, even though independent studies and audits have repeatedly found such cases to be extremely rare. A federal judge has already blocked key parts of the order from taking effect while litigation over its constitutionality continues, but the whistleblower alleges the Postal Service has continued quietly building out the system anyway, potentially in violation of that court order.

Blumenthal, who has emerged as one of the sharpest critics of the plan, said the disclosure shows the agency has effectively designed a system that is likely to fail Americans rather than protect the integrity of their votes. He described the technical shortcuts alleged in the whistleblower's account as "mind-boggling" and said he found it difficult to view the rushed rollout, timed for a September 1 implementation target, as anything other than reckless given how directly it could affect voters' ability to cast a ballot in a race already expected to be closely contested nationwide.
The White House pushes back

A Postal Service spokesperson defended the new system, describing it as part of a broader, year-round effort to ensure election mail is handled securely and efficiently, and characterizing the portal as a simple tool to help state election officials share information about voters receiving mail ballots. The White House has also disputed the whistleblower's characterization of the rollout, though officials have not offered a detailed technical rebuttal of the specific failure scenario described in the disclosure.

With mail voting for the midterms already beginning in several states, the dispute is likely to intensify quickly rather than play out over a leisurely legislative timeline. Voting rights advocates say the coming weeks will be a crucial test of whether the courts can act fast enough to prevent any large-scale disruption before ballots are due, while lawmakers on the relevant committees have indicated they plan further oversight hearings to press Postal Service leadership on exactly how extensively the disputed system has already been deployed despite the ongoing legal challenge.

Election officials in several states have said they are closely monitoring the situation and preparing contingency plans in case the disputed system is allowed to proceed despite the ongoing legal challenge. Voting rights organizations have urged voters who plan to cast ballots by mail to request them as early as possible and to track their status closely, given the uncertainty surrounding how smoothly the new verification process might ultimately function once it is put into practice.

us.metaTitle: Miami Cargo Plane Crash: NTSB Details Go-Around Attempt
us.title: Flight Data Shows Amazon Cargo Jet Attempted Late Go-Around Before Deadly Miami Runway Crash
us.metaDescription: NTSB flight data shows the Amazon 767 briefly tried to abort its landing before overrunning a Miami runway and killing five people in a ground vehicle.
us.excerpt: New flight data released by the NTSB shows the Amazon-operated Boeing 767 briefly attempted a go-around before overrunning a Miami International Airport runway, killing five people in a cleaning crew van.
us.imageAlt: Investigators examine the wreckage of a cargo plane that overran the runway at Miami International Airport
keyTakeaways: NTSB flight data shows the Amazon-operated Boeing 767 briefly attempted a go-around, with throttles increasing to power settings consistent with an aborted landing before the crew tried again to stop the plane.
The aircraft, operating as 21 Air Flight 7598, overran runway 30 at roughly 158 knots and traveled about 1,300 feet past the runway's end before striking a van and an SUV.
Five people riding in a plane-cleaning company's van were killed; five others were hurt, with two still in critical condition as of Tuesday.
Investigators say the plane's thrust reversers were never deployed, and they plan to interview both pilots on Wednesday to understand the crew's decision-making in the final seconds.
Miami International Airport meets FAA minimum safety buffer requirements but lacks the crushable runway-arrestor material used at more than 120 other U.S. airports.
The airport reopened a third runway Tuesday evening, though the full NTSB investigation and final report are expected to take a year or longer.

content.text: Newly released flight data indicates the pilots of an Amazon-operated cargo jet tried to pull out of a rocky landing at Miami International Airport moments before the plane overshot the runway, struck a work van and killed five people, federal investigators said Tuesday. The disclosure, made during an evening briefing by the National Transportation Safety Board, offers the clearest picture yet of what unfolded in the final seconds before Sunday's crash, though officials cautioned that key questions about the crew's decisions remain unanswered until pilot interviews take place this week.
What Happened During the Landing Attempt

The Boeing 767-300, operating as 21 Air Flight 7598 on behalf of Amazon Air, was completing the third leg of a busy flight schedule that had taken it from Cincinnati to Miami, on to San Juan, Puerto Rico, and back again when it came in for landing on runway 30 around 2 p.m. Sunday. Instead of stopping within the runway's length, the jet continued roughly 1,300 feet past its end, tore through a perimeter fence and struck a parked SUV on a nearby city street after first colliding with a van on airport property. The wreckage, along with both damaged vehicles, remained at the scene through Tuesday as investigators worked to document the site.
Flight Data Reveals a Late Go-Around Attempt

NTSB lead investigator Chihoon Shin walked reporters through a timeline pulled from the flight data recorder. About 30 seconds before the recording ends, the plane's nose and right main landing gear touched down with the aircraft traveling at 158 knots. Brakes were applied 23 seconds before the end of the recording, then released 15 seconds later at a ground speed of 120 knots, at which point the throttles advanced to settings consistent with an attempted go-around. NTSB Chairwoman Jennifer Homendy said the crew appeared to briefly try to abort the landing and climb away before reversing course again and attempting to bring the plane to a stop. Notably, she said, the data showed the thrust reversers, a key tool for slowing a jet on the runway, were never engaged.
Aviation Experts Weigh In on the Pilots' Actions

Outside experts reviewing the limited public data said the sequence points to an unstable approach from the outset. Former FAA official Mike O'Donnell said the plane touching down nose and right gear first was itself a sign of trouble, and that any decision to go around should have come earlier. Once the crew committed to stopping instead, he said, there may not have been enough runway left to avoid an overrun. Aviation attorney Mary Schiavo, a former Transportation Department inspector general, said the back-and-forth in the flight data hints at confusion in the cockpit over which course of action to take, a detail investigators hope Wednesday's interviews with both pilots will clarify.
Pilots Set to Be Interviewed Wednesday

Both crew members have been identified by officials: Captain Joseph Carroll, 55, who had logged roughly 7,145 flight hours as of the end of March, and First Officer Jaime Felipe Silva Molina, 37, who had about 2,655 hours as of late August. Both men were treated and released from the hospital, according to Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz. Homendy said the agency deliberately held off releasing details from the cockpit voice recorder, which captured more than two hours of usable audio, until investigators can sit down with the pilots directly and hear their account of what they were doing and why.
Weather and Runway Conditions Under Review

Storms were building near the airport as the flight arrived from San Juan, and investigators say a tailwind may have pushed the aircraft further down the runway than intended. That has raised questions about why air traffic control had the plane landing in that direction rather than switching the approach to give pilots a headwind, a decision investigators plan to examine closely along with whatever weather briefing the crew received before the final approach.
Victims and Injuries From the Crash

All five people who died were riding in a van operated by Professional Ocean Service Corp., a contractor that cleans aircraft for airlines at MIA. The van, which was carrying seven people at the time, was struck first as the jet skidded off the runway. The Miami-Dade Sheriff's Office identified the victims as Rolando Aleman Leon, 55; Yoel Rodriguez Naranjo, 53; Julio C. Pineda, 75; Carlos Acosta Fajardo, 53; and Javierkys Reyes Quevedo, 47. Five other people were hurt in the crash; as of Tuesday, two remained in critical condition and a third was listed as stable. In a statement, Professional Ocean Service Corp. said its workers were "far more than the people who work beside us each day," and asked for privacy as families grieve. Amazon said it is cooperating fully with investigators and extended condolences to the victims and their families.
Airport Safety Concerns and Runway Arrestor Systems

Homendy said investigators will examine whether the absence of a runway arrestor system at Miami International Airport contributed to the severity of the crash. More than 120 U.S. airports use lightweight, crushable material at the end of runways designed to safely stop planes that overrun their landing strip, a system the FAA credits with saving roughly 500 lives. Miami does not have that technology, though other aviation experts note the airport still satisfies FAA rules requiring a minimum 1,000-foot buffer zone past each runway's end. Homendy said runway excursions remain a persistent problem nationally despite years of safety recommendations, and that preventing the next one depends on airports and regulators acting on the findings investigators eventually produce.
The Aircraft's History From Passenger Jet to Cargo Plane

The 767 involved in Sunday's crash was originally built to carry passengers and flew for multiple foreign airlines for more than two decades before it was converted into a cargo aircraft in 2015, according to flight-tracking data. It was operated by 21 Air, a Miami-based cargo carrier, on behalf of Amazon's Prime Air delivery network. Investigators say the aircraft's age and ownership history will be reviewed as part of the broader probe, though officials have not suggested the plane's history played a direct role in the crash.
Impact on Flights and Airport Operations

The crash forced Miami International Airport to briefly close all four of its runways and triggered a ground stop that rippled through the airport's schedule for two days. More than 225 flights were canceled Sunday and Monday, with hundreds more delayed, before the NTSB released a third runway back to airport operators Tuesday evening. Several airlines, including American Airlines, waived change fees for travelers affected by the disruption, and airport officials urged passengers to check flight status directly with their carriers while cleanup and the investigation continue near the fourth runway.
What Investigators Will Examine Next

With Wednesday's pilot interviews approaching, the NTSB's roughly 32-person investigative team is continuing to document wreckage, collect perishable evidence and interview air traffic controllers, dispatchers and ground witnesses. Homendy has said the agency will not determine a probable cause while still on scene, and a final report identifying what went wrong and recommending changes to prevent future runway excursions is not expected for a year or more. In the meantime, the agency said it will work to return the remaining closed runway to normal service as quickly as the investigation allows.

finance.metaTitle: Fed rate-hike odds jump under Chair Warsh as oil shock stokes inflation fears
finance.title: Fed rate-hike odds jump under Chair Warsh as oil shock stokes inflation fears
finance.metaDescription: Traders now see a much higher chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase this month after oil prices surged, reversing expectations that had leaned toward a hold just a week earlier.
finance.excerpt: Traders now see a much higher chance of a Federal Reserve rate increase this month after oil prices surged, reversing expectations that had leaned toward a hold just a week earlier.
finance.imageAlt: Federal Reserve building representing shifting expectations for an interest rate hike
keyTakeaways: Markets now price a roughly 66% chance of a Fed rate hike this month
That figure has flipped from a majority expecting a hold just a week earlier
Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has described the economy as solid despite the pressure

content.text: Expectations for the Federal Reserve's next move have shifted dramatically over the past week, with traders now pricing in a roughly two-thirds chance that the central bank will raise interest rates later this month, a sharp reversal from just days earlier when the majority of market participants expected policymakers to hold steady. The shift comes as oil prices have surged amid renewed conflict between the United States and Iran, reviving inflation concerns that had appeared to be easing over the summer.

According to data tracked by the CME Group's widely followed FedWatch tool, the probability of a quarter-point rate increase this month climbed to roughly 66%, up from about 40% just a week prior. That kind of rapid swing underscores how sensitive monetary policy expectations have become to developments in the Middle East, where the latest round of fighting near the Strait of Hormuz has pushed crude prices to their highest level in more than a month.
Warsh weighs growth against inflation risk

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh has characterized the underlying US economy as solid, pointing to robust business investment, steady consumer spending and labor market conditions broadly consistent with full employment during recent public remarks. That relatively upbeat assessment stands in contrast to concerns raised by some economists earlier this summer, when a disappointing jobs report and downward revisions to prior months' hiring figures had briefly stoked fears that the labor market was weakening more sharply than previously understood.

The renewed spike in energy prices complicates that picture considerably. Inflation remains elevated relative to the Fed's 2% target, a gap the central bank has partly attributed to supply shocks affecting specific sectors, including energy. With oil now trading well above $90 a barrel amid the ongoing conflict, policymakers face a genuinely difficult balancing act between supporting a labor market that has shown signs of softening and containing price pressures that could become more entrenched the longer elevated energy costs persist.
Markets brace for a consequential decision

The stakes of the upcoming decision extend well beyond the immediate rate move itself. Global government bond yields have already climbed to multi-year highs in anticipation of tighter policy, with the 10-year Treasury yield hovering around 4.78% and longer-dated yields pushing back toward levels last seen more than a decade ago. Higher borrowing costs of that magnitude ripple through mortgage rates, corporate financing costs and equity valuations, making the Fed's next move one of the more closely watched events on the calendar for both Wall Street and Main Street alike.

Economists remain divided on which way the Fed will ultimately lean. Some argue that a still-resilient labor market and the risk of inflation expectations becoming unanchored justify moving forward with a hike despite the recent softness in hiring data. Others caution that raising rates into an energy-driven price shock, rather than one rooted in broader demand pressures, risks unnecessarily choking off growth just as consumers are already contending with higher gasoline and heating costs. With the decision still weeks away, traders say the coming data releases, including fresh inflation and employment figures, are likely to keep shifting the odds right up until the Fed's announcement.

Regional Fed officials have offered somewhat differing public assessments of the appropriate path forward, reflecting the genuine uncertainty within the institution itself about how to weigh the competing risks. Some have emphasized the importance of not overreacting to what could prove to be a temporary, geopolitically driven spike in prices, while others have argued that allowing inflation expectations to drift higher, even temporarily, could prove more costly to unwind later than the short-term pain of tighter policy now.

Financial commentators have also noted the unusual optics of a central bank potentially raising rates even as some labor market indicators point toward softness, a combination that has historically been relatively rare and that adds an additional layer of scrutiny to whatever decision the Fed ultimately reaches at its upcoming meeting.

finance.metaTitle: Nvidia Q2 Earnings Crush Estimates on AI Chip Demand
finance.title: Nvidia's AI Chip Demand Drives Q2 Earnings Past Estimates
finance.metaDescription: Nvidia posted $96.22 billion in Q2 revenue and $59.69 billion in net income, beating Wall Street estimates as AI chip and data center demand surged.
finance.excerpt: Nvidia's latest quarterly results topped Wall Street's expectations by a wide margin, with data center revenue more than doubling as hyperscalers continue pouring capital into AI infrastructure despite growing questions about the pace of spending.
finance.imageAlt: Nvidia AI data center GPU chips powering artificial intelligence infrastructure for hyperscale cloud providers
keyTakeaways: Nvidia reported fiscal Q2 net income of $59.69 billion and revenue of $96.22 billion, both far exceeding Wall Street estimates, as data center revenue more than doubled to $89 billion.
CEO Jensen Huang said the company's supply chain is meeting only about 70% of demand, even as Nvidia forecasts $108 billion in revenue for the current quarter and 70% revenue growth for fiscal 2028.

Despite the strong results, Nvidia shares fell 1.6% during the regular session before rising 4.1% after hours, reflecting ongoing investor debate over how long the AI infrastructure spending boom can continue.

content.text: Nvidia once again delivered quarterly results that outpaced Wall Street's expectations, reporting fiscal second-quarter revenue of $96.22 billion and net income of $59.69 billion as demand for its high-end artificial intelligence chips continued to outstrip the company's ability to supply them. The results, released Wednesday, mark the latest evidence that spending on AI infrastructure by major technology companies remains robust even as some investors grow more cautious about how long the current pace of investment can be sustained.

Net income for the May-to-July period nearly tripled from $26.42 billion a year earlier, translating to earnings of $2.46 per share. Stripping out certain one-time items, adjusted earnings came in at $2.22 per share, comfortably ahead of the $2.09 per share analysts had projected, according to FactSet consensus estimates compiled ahead of the report. Revenue more than doubled year over year and topped the average Wall Street forecast of $92.27 billion.
Earnings and Revenue Growth Beat Wall Street Forecasts

Nvidia's net income figure included a $7.8 billion gain tied to the company's equity investments in other firms, including stakes in Intel and SpaceX, following a similar $15.9 billion gain in the prior quarter. Those investment gains added to an already strong operating performance driven by chip sales, underscoring how Nvidia has increasingly used its cash position to take equity stakes in strategically important partners across the technology and aerospace sectors.

"AI has reached its inflection point. It's doing useful work. Its tokens are productive and profitable. Now, compute is revenue," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in a statement accompanying the results. The comment reflects a shift in how Nvidia frames its business, from selling chips primarily for AI model training toward positioning its hardware as the backbone of AI systems that are now generating measurable economic output for customers.
Data Center Business Fuels the Bulk of Growth

Nvidia's data center segment, which includes AI-focused data center hardware and chip sales to hyperscale cloud operators such as Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Meta, generated $89 billion in revenue, more than double what it produced a year earlier and ahead of analyst expectations of roughly $86.33 billion. The segment now accounts for approximately 92% of Nvidia's total revenue, reflecting how thoroughly the company's business has become concentrated around AI infrastructure demand relative to its more traditional gaming and graphics chip roots.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress told analysts on the earnings call that capital spending among the top five hyperscale cloud providers is projected to reach nearly $800 billion this year and climb to roughly $1.3 trillion in 2027, underscoring the scale of AI infrastructure investment that continues to flow toward companies like Nvidia. On the day of the earnings release, Nvidia and Amazon Web Services separately announced plans to deploy 2 million additional Nvidia graphics processing units, along with an agreement to incorporate Nvidia chips into Amazon's fleet of warehouse robots.
Supply Constraints Are Limiting How Fast Nvidia Can Grow

Even with blockbuster results, Nvidia's leadership emphasized that the company's growth remains capped by how much product it can actually manufacture and ship. "Our entire supply chain is challenged," Huang told analysts. "At this point we have supply for 70%. ... Our demand is much higher than that." Kress echoed that point, noting that Nvidia's growth outlook for its next fiscal year would be closer to double the projected 70% rate if supply constraints weren't limiting how much of that demand the company can currently fulfill, based on forecasts shared by its own customers.

Operating expenses climbed alongside revenue, rising 55% year over year to $8.41 billion, reflecting the scale of investment Nvidia is making in research, staffing and supply chain commitments to keep pace with demand. The company also disclosed that its supply commitments, largely tied to memory procurement, more than doubled from $119 billion in the prior quarter to $279 billion in the most recent period, a sign of how aggressively Nvidia is locking in manufacturing capacity to support future growth.
Forward Guidance Points to Accelerating Growth

For the current quarter, Nvidia forecast revenue of approximately $108 billion, ahead of the $104.86 billion analysts had penciled in. Meeting that target would represent an increase of roughly 89% from the same period last year, suggesting Nvidia's growth rate is still accelerating rather than slowing as the AI infrastructure buildout matures. Notably, the company said its outlook assumes no data center compute revenue from China, reflecting the ongoing impact of export restrictions on that market.

Looking further ahead, Nvidia said it expects revenue for its fiscal year ending January 2028 to grow by approximately 70%, a figure that itself surprised some analysts who had been modeling slower growth deceleration heading into that period. Kress also said the company expects its central processing unit revenue to more than double in fiscal 2028, a shift the company said would position it as one of the world's leading server CPU suppliers alongside its dominant position in AI accelerators.
Capital Returns and Shareholder Payouts

Alongside its growth investments, Nvidia continued returning capital to shareholders, spending $26 billion on share repurchases and dividends during the quarter. The company previously told investors in May that it had authorized an additional $80 billion in buybacks, and it also announced plans to pay a 25-cent-per-share dividend, continuing a pattern of increased capital returns as both revenue and free cash flow have expanded rapidly in recent years.
How Markets and Investors Reacted

Nvidia shares initially closed the regular trading session down 1.6% on the day of the report, before climbing 4.1% in after-hours trading once the results and guidance were released. The stock is up 12.4% so far this year, a more modest gain relative to Nvidia's outsized rallies in prior years of the AI boom, reflecting a market that has grown somewhat more measured in how it prices in the company's continued outperformance.

The company's edge computing segment, which covers chips that bring AI capabilities to personal computers, gaming consoles and robotics, posted revenue of $7.2 billion, up 27% from the same period a year earlier. While a much smaller contributor than the data center business, the segment reflects Nvidia's continued push to extend AI processing capability beyond large cloud data centers and into a broader range of consumer and industrial devices.
Questions About AI Spending Sustainability Persist

Despite the strength of the results, a segment of investors and analysts remain cautious about the durability of the current AI investment cycle. Nvidia's market valuation has climbed from roughly $400 billion at the end of 2022 to approximately $5.2 trillion today, a rise that has made the company one of the most closely watched bellwethers for the broader technology sector and for AI-driven market gains more broadly.

finance.metaTitle: US Sanctions Turkish Bank Over Iran Oil Network
finance.title: US Treasury Sanctions Small Turkish Bank in Widening Campaign to Choke Off Iran's Financial Lifelines
finance.metaDescription: The US Treasury sanctioned a Turkish investment bank and two affiliates for allegedly moving Iranian oil revenue, the first NATO-country bank hit in the campaign.
finance.excerpt: The Treasury Department has sanctioned an Istanbul-based investment bank and two related firms for allegedly helping move Iranian oil revenue through China and Turkey. It's the first time a bank based in a NATO member country has been targeted in the current pressure campaign against Tehran.
finance.imageAlt: Istanbul skyline with a financial district backdrop symbolizing US sanctions on a Turkish bank tied to Iran
keyTakeaways: The Treasury Department designated Istanbul-based Golden Global Yatirim Bankasi and two affiliated firms for allegedly helping route Iranian oil revenue from China through Turkey, cutting the entities off from the dollar-based financial system.

It marks the first time a bank headquartered in a NATO member country has been sanctioned under the current U.S. pressure campaign against Iran, a signal Washington is willing to extend financial penalties to allied nations.

Sanctions experts are split on the impact, noting the targeted bank is small but the action could deter other financial institutions from doing business with it, even as some question whether the pressure will change the trajectory of the broader conflict with Iran.

content.text: The U.S. Treasury Department has escalated its financial pressure campaign against Iran by sanctioning a small Turkish investment bank and two of its affiliated firms, marking the first time a lender based in a NATO member country has been targeted since Washington intensified its efforts to cut off Tehran's revenue streams. The designations, announced Friday, hit Istanbul-based Golden Global Yatirim Bankasi Anonim Sirketi along with an affiliated asset manager and an asset leasing company, all accused of helping move Iranian oil proceeds through China and into the Turkish financial system.
What the Treasury Alleges About Golden Global's Role

According to the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control, Golden Global and its affiliates were structured to give Iran's shadow banking network a way to convert oil revenue earned from Chinese buyers into hard currency and gold once it reached Turkey. OFAC said the bank offered correspondent banking services to Iranian financial institutions, allowing transactions to flow through accounts tied to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' Qods Force and a network previously sanctioned in 2022 that includes Turkish businessman Sitki Ayan.

All three entities have now been added to the Specially Designated Nationals list, which effectively bars them from accessing the U.S. dollar-based financial system and from doing business with American companies or individuals. The Treasury did issue a general license permitting the wind-down of existing transactions, a standard step meant to give counterparties time to unwind exposure without triggering immediate secondary violations.
A Turkish Bank Pushes Back

Golden Global Yatirim Bankasi, ranked as Turkey's 35th-largest bank by assets, rejected the allegations outright, saying it has met local and international compliance standards and would pursue legal action over what it called baseless claims. The bank also said none of the individuals or entities named in the Treasury's order were among its customers and that it had no direct or indirect dealings with them. Public banking data show the lender held roughly 25 billion Turkish lira, or about $517 million, in total assets last year, underscoring how small the institution is relative to Turkey's major state and commercial banks.
Why Targeting a NATO-Country Bank Matters

The decision to sanction a Turkish-based institution carries symbolic weight beyond the size of the bank itself. Turkey is a NATO member and a longtime U.S. ally, and until now the current sanctions campaign against Iran had avoided directly targeting banks headquartered in allied nations. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent framed the action as part of a broader effort to squeeze Tehran's finances, saying the message was meant for any institution believed to be facilitating trade with Iran and the Revolutionary Guard, and adding that Washington intends to keep working with allies until it has "buried the head of the Iranian snake."

Bessent also tied the sanctions to the broader U.S. naval posture in the Persian Gulf, saying the ongoing blockade of the Strait of Hormuz has stranded Iranian crude shipments meant for Chinese buyers. With tankers unable to unload and onboard storage filling up, he argued Iran's oil export revenue is shrinking just as it needs cash to sustain its military campaign. He also indicated on a separate broadcast that additional sanctions against another bank could be announced within days.
Part of a Broader Pattern of Financial Pressure

Friday's action follows months of expanding Treasury measures aimed at Iran's so-called shadow banking network, which has relied on intermediaries across Asia, the Gulf and Europe to move oil revenue outside the traditional, more easily monitored banking system. Earlier this year, Treasury sanctioned dozens of entities and vessels tied to similar oil-smuggling and money-laundering networks, and last week it moved to restrict an Egyptian lender's overseas branches from U.S. dollar transactions over their dealings with Iran, though that penalty stopped short of touching the bank's headquarters or other branches.
Analysts Weigh the Real-World Impact

Sanctions specialists say the significance of the move lies less in the size of Golden Global's balance sheet than in the signal it sends to other financial institutions operating in Turkey and the wider region. Miad Maleki, a sanctions expert at the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies, said the action makes clear that Turkey is now viewed as a likely conduit for Iranian money as Gulf routes are choked off, and that Washington is prepared to act there directly. He added that any foreign bank that continues doing business with the sanctioned Turkish entity risks exposure of its own, calling that ripple effect the real purpose behind targeting a relatively small lender.

Other observers are more skeptical that individual sanctions actions like this one will meaningfully alter the course of the conflict. Brett Erickson, managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors, said the designation would only modestly raise the cost of doing business for Iran, cautioning that "hurting Iran and changing the outcome of this war are two very different things." He warned that if the broader sanctions campaign fails to shift Iran's economic calculus, Washington risks provoking retaliation that could carry far greater consequences for global markets than the sanctions themselves.
What Comes Next

With Bessent suggesting more sanctions could follow within days, markets and foreign banks are likely to watch closely for signs of which institutions in Turkey, the Gulf and Asia might be next in line. The broader question for investors is whether this incremental pressure campaign — paired with the ongoing naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz — will be enough to bring Iran back to the negotiating table, or whether it primarily adds friction and risk to global oil and financial markets without resolving the underlying conflict. Either outcome carries implications for energy prices, shipping costs and financial institutions with any exposure to Iran-linked trade routes.

finance.metaTitle: August Jobs Report: US Adds 162,000 Jobs, Lifting Fed Rate-Hike Odds
finance.title: US Economy Adds 162,000 Jobs in August, More Than Double Forecasts, Boosting Fed Rate-Hike Bets
finance.metaDescription: Nonfarm payrolls rose 162,000 in August, far exceeding forecasts, as the unemployment rate held at 4.1% and traders raised the odds of a Federal Reserve rate hike at this month's policy meeting.
finance.excerpt: The US added 162,000 jobs in August, more than double what economists expected, pushing traders to raise their bets on a Federal Reserve rate increase at this month's meeting even as next week's inflation data looms as the bigger swing factor.
finance.imageAlt: A now hiring sign displayed outside a US business storefront
keyTakeaways: US employers added 162,000 jobs in August, more than double the roughly 56,000 economists had forecast, while unemployment held steady at 4.1%.
July's figure was revised from a loss of 23,000 jobs to a gain of 21,000, and June was also revised upward, pointing to a stronger underlying labor market than initially reported.
Traders raised the odds of a Fed rate hike at the September 15-16 meeting to roughly 60%, though next week's inflation data is expected to be the more decisive factor.

content.text: The U.S. labor market delivered a surprisingly strong reading heading into the fall, complicating the outlook for the Federal Reserve just weeks before its next policy meeting. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that employers added 162,000 jobs in August, more than double the roughly 56,000 to 65,000 gain economists had forecast, while the unemployment rate held steady at 4.1%.

The rebound followed a sluggish stretch of hiring over the summer. July's initially reported loss of 23,000 jobs was revised sharply upward to a gain of 21,000, and June's tally was also revised higher, adding another 11,000 positions to the total. Taken together, the revisions and the August beat paint a picture of a labor market that, while cooler than the breakneck hiring pace of a few years ago, remains considerably more resilient than the anemic summer figures had suggested.
Where the jobs came from

The gains were broad-based across several sectors. Local government education added roughly 42,000 positions as the 2026-27 school year got underway, a seasonal pattern tied to teachers returning to payrolls after the summer break. Food service and drinking establishments added 59,000 jobs, continuing to serve as one of the economy's most reliable sources of hiring. Construction added 22,000 positions and healthcare contributed another 12,000, rounding out a report that showed strength concentrated in service-oriented and public-sector categories rather than any single standout industry.

Average hourly earnings rose 3.1% from a year earlier, slightly ahead of the roughly 3% economists had expected, while the labor force participation rate ticked up to 61.6%, even though it remains half a percentage point below where it stood at the start of the year. The employment-to-population ratio held largely steady at 59.1%, suggesting only modest underlying shifts in how many working-age Americans are actively employed.
Fed rate-hike odds climb

Markets moved quickly to reassess the odds of a Federal Reserve interest rate increase at the central bank's September 15-16 policy meeting. According to data tracked by the CME Group's FedWatch tool, traders were pricing in roughly 60% odds of a quarter-point hike following the report, up meaningfully from expectations just days earlier that had leaned toward the Fed holding rates steady. Treasury yields, particularly at shorter maturities most sensitive to Fed policy, climbed following the release, while stock futures initially dipped as investors weighed the prospect of tighter monetary policy.

Ellen Zentner, chief economic strategist at Morgan Stanley Wealth Management, said the upside surprise in payrolls would likely intensify concerns about a near-term rate increase, but cautioned that the outcome ultimately rests on next week's inflation data. If the Consumer Price Index report due out shortly before the Fed's meeting comes in cooler than expected, she said, policymakers may feel comfortable looking past the stronger labor market reading. Atsi Sheth, chief credit officer at Moody's Ratings, echoed that view, noting that Friday's employment figures were just one of the final pieces of data the Fed will weigh before its meeting, with the CPI report standing as the more decisive input.
A labor market defined by contradictions

The report adds another layer of complexity to a labor market that has sent mixed signals throughout much of the year. Sectors tied to information technology have shown job losses in recent months, which some economists attribute partly to companies redirecting investment toward artificial intelligence infrastructure rather than headcount. At the same time, traditionally lower-wage service sectors like food service and hospitality have continued adding positions at a healthy clip, illustrating an uneven recovery across different corners of the economy.

For consumers and businesses alike, the report reinforces a familiar pattern this year: incoming data has proven difficult to interpret cleanly, with strength in one area frequently offset by weakness in another. That ambiguity leaves the Federal Reserve's next move harder to predict than it might otherwise be, with officials expected to weigh this report alongside inflation data, oil-price pressures tied to geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, and broader signals about consumer spending before finalizing their decision later this month.

finance.metaTitle: Oracle Earnings Preview: Can the $638 Billion AI Backlog Ease Investor Worries?
finance.title: Oracle's Record AI Backlog Faces Its Next Test as Fiscal Q1 Earnings Approach
finance.metaDescription: Oracle reports fiscal first-quarter 2027 results on September 10, with investors watching whether its record $638 billion AI infrastructure backlog can offset concerns about negative free cash flow and heavy capital spending.
finance.excerpt: Oracle reports quarterly earnings this week carrying a record $638 billion AI contract backlog, but investors remain focused on whether the company's massive capital spending plans and negative free cash flow can be sustained.
finance.imageAlt: Oracle corporate office building signage ahead of the company's quarterly earnings report
keyTakeaways: Oracle reports fiscal Q1 2027 earnings on September 10, with analysts forecasting EPS of $1.74 on revenue near $19.1 billion.
The company's remaining performance obligations, a measure of contracted future revenue, reached $638 billion last quarter, up 363% year over year.
Oracle shares are down more than 20% in 2026 despite record growth, as investors weigh negative free cash flow of over $13 billion against plans to raise $45-50 billion for data center expansion.

content.text: Oracle is set to report fiscal first-quarter 2027 results after markets close on September 10, a report Wall Street is watching as a test of whether the company's enormous artificial intelligence infrastructure backlog can keep translating into the kind of growth that has justified its soaring valuation this year. Analysts are forecasting earnings of roughly $1.74 per share on revenue near $19.1 billion, according to consensus estimates compiled by financial data providers.

The report arrives against an unusual backdrop. Oracle shares have actually declined more than 20% so far in 2026 even as the company posted record revenue growth throughout the year, a disconnect that reflects investor anxiety about how the company plans to fund its aggressive data-center expansion rather than doubts about underlying demand.
A backlog too large to ignore

At the center of the story is Oracle's remaining performance obligations, a figure that tracks contracted future revenue the company has not yet recognized. That backlog swelled to $638 billion by the end of the prior quarter, up 363% from a year earlier and an increase of $85 billion in just the final quarter alone. Company executives have said the bulk of that growth stems from large-scale AI infrastructure contracts, many of which involve customers either prepaying Oracle for graphics processing units or supplying the hardware themselves, arrangements that lock in future revenue but also reshape how quickly Oracle's cash flow statement reflects that demand.

Oracle's cloud infrastructure business, the segment most directly tied to renting out computing capacity to AI developers, has been the standout performer. In the most recent quarter reported, cloud infrastructure revenue climbed 93% year over year to $5.8 billion, part of total cloud revenue of $9.9 billion that grew 47%. For the current quarter, the company has guided for total cloud revenue growth between 57% and 64% year over year, a pace that, if achieved, would extend a run of accelerating growth that has made Oracle one of the more closely tracked bellwethers for AI infrastructure spending broadly.
The funding question investors keep asking

That growth has come at a steep cost. Oracle reported negative free cash flow of more than $13 billion over the trailing twelve months as it pours money into new data centers, and the company has said it plans to raise between $45 billion and $50 billion in additional funding this fiscal year to keep expanding capacity, with plans for more than 10 gigawatts of new computing power coming online over the next three years. Executives have said they do not expect to raise additional debt funding during the 2026 calendar year, but analysts continue to press the company on how sustainable its capital spending plans are given the gap between what it is investing and the cash its operations currently generate.

Renting out Nvidia's graphics processing units to AI companies also carries thinner profit margins than Oracle's traditional software licensing business, adding another layer of scrutiny to how the numbers ultimately flow through to the bottom line even as top-line growth impresses. The company has previously raised its full-year revenue forecast by roughly $1 billion to around $90 billion, ahead of the roughly $86.6 billion analysts had been modeling, a sign of confidence from management even as questions about financing persist.
Big-name customers and a crowded field

Oracle has touted a customer roster that includes Air France-KLM, Lockheed Martin, SoftBank and Microsoft's Activision Blizzard gaming unit, part of a broader push to diversify its cloud infrastructure client base beyond the handful of AI labs that have driven headlines this year. The company also continues to expand multicloud partnerships with rivals Amazon, Google and Microsoft, an arrangement that has produced explosive growth in database revenue shared across those platforms even as Oracle competes with those same companies for broader cloud infrastructure spending.

For investors, Thursday's report is likely to hinge less on whether Oracle beats consensus estimates -- the company has a strong recent track record of doing so -- and more on what management says about capital spending discipline, backlog conversion timelines, and margin trajectory as data centers built this year begin contributing more fully to revenue. With Oracle's stock having lagged the broader AI infrastructure rally despite record contract growth, how the market interprets Thursday's commentary could determine whether that gap starts to close.

finance.metaTitle: Mortgage Rates Near One-Year High as Bond Market Reacts to Jobs Data
finance.title: Mortgage Rates Climb Toward One-Year Highs as Strong Jobs Data Rattles Bond Markets
finance.metaDescription: The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate has risen to 6.74%, near its highest level in a year, as a stronger-than-expected jobs report and rising oil prices push Treasury yields higher ahead of the Fed's September meeting.
finance.excerpt: Mortgage rates are hovering near a one-year high after a stronger-than-expected jobs report and rising oil prices pushed Treasury yields up, squeezing affordability for buyers just as the Fed's September meeting approaches.
finance.imageAlt: A for sale sign in front of a suburban US home as mortgage rates climb toward one-year highs
keyTakeaways: The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate stands at 6.74%, just under its one-year high of 6.78% touched earlier this month, according to Optimal Blue data.
Refinance rates have climbed even faster, with the 30-year fixed refinance average jumping to 7.31%, up roughly 34 basis points in a single week.
Major forecasters now expect 30-year rates to stay between 6.6% and 6.8% through the end of 2026 and into 2027, dimming hopes for a return to sub-5% rates.

content.text: Mortgage rates have climbed to some of their highest levels of the past year, adding pressure to an already strained housing market just as buyers head into the traditionally slower fall selling season. The average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage stood at 6.74% as markets reopened this week following the Labor Day holiday, according to Optimal Blue data, hovering just under the one-year high of 6.78% touched earlier this month.

Freddie Mac's separate weekly survey, which uses a different methodology, put the 30-year fixed rate at 6.71% as of September 3, up from 6.66% the prior week and from 6.50% at this time last year. Refinance rates have moved even more sharply: the national average 30-year fixed refinance rate jumped to 7.31% earlier this week, according to Zillow data, a climb of roughly 34 basis points from the prior week's average.
Why rates keep climbing

Unlike the Federal Reserve's short-term policy rate, mortgage rates track more closely with the yield on the 10-year Treasury note, which has risen amid a mix of factors weighing on bond markets this year. A stronger-than-expected August jobs report added to the recent pressure, since robust hiring data reduces the odds that the Federal Reserve will cut rates and instead raises the possibility of a rate increase at its September 15-16 meeting, a dynamic that tends to push longer-term borrowing costs higher rather than lower. Rising oil prices tied to renewed tensions in the Middle East have also stoked broader inflation concerns, adding another layer of pressure on the bond market that feeds directly into mortgage pricing.

Housing analysts note that mortgage rates and Fed policy do not move in lockstep the way many borrowers assume. Even if the Fed opts to raise rates this month, mortgage rates could in theory ease somewhat if that decision helps convince bond investors that inflation is being brought under control over the longer term. Conversely, a Fed decision to hold rates steady could still coincide with higher mortgage rates if investors interpret that restraint as evidence that inflation risks remain elevated. That disconnect has made forecasting mortgage costs an unusually difficult exercise this year, even for economists closely tracking the incoming data.
What higher rates mean for the housing market

The practical impact on borrowers is significant. At a 6.74% rate, a $400,000 mortgage carries a monthly principal and interest payment of roughly $2,592, and a $320,000 loan on a $400,000 home purchased with 20% down runs about $2,073 a month. Compared with a year ago, when rates hovered closer to 6.50%, that translates into tens of dollars more in monthly payments and thousands of additional dollars over the life of a typical loan -- a gap that continues to squeeze affordability for prospective buyers already contending with elevated home prices in many markets.

Major forecasters, including Fannie Mae and the Mortgage Bankers Association, have recently revised their long-term rate projections, now expecting 30-year rates to remain in a range of roughly 6.6% to 6.8% through the end of 2026 and well into 2027. That outlook suggests borrowers hoping for a meaningful pullback toward the sub-5% rates seen earlier this decade are likely to be waiting considerably longer than many had hoped, reshaping expectations across the real estate industry.
What comes next for rate watchers

The coming days carry several data points capable of moving mortgage rates further in either direction. A Producer Price Index report is due September 10, followed by the more closely watched Consumer Price Index reading for August on September 11, both arriving just before the Federal Reserve's policy decision on September 16. Mortgage industry analysts generally advise borrowers within 45 days of closing to consider locking in a rate given the current elevated and volatile environment, while those with more flexible timelines are encouraged to watch how lenders reprice following each new economic release rather than reacting to any single day's headline number.

finance.metaTitle: SEC Sues Proxy Adviser ISS as Trump Administration Escalates Oversight
finance.title: SEC Sues Institutional Shareholder Services to Enforce Subpoena Amid Trump-Era Proxy Adviser Crackdown
finance.metaDescription: The SEC has filed a subpoena-enforcement lawsuit against proxy adviser ISS, escalating a Trump administration push to scrutinize the firms that shape how institutional investors vote at shareholder meetings.
finance.excerpt: The SEC has sued Institutional Shareholder Services to compel it to hand over years of proxy voting data, intensifying a Trump administration campaign targeting the influential advisers that shape shareholder votes at public companies.
finance.imageAlt: Exterior of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission headquarters building in Washington, DC
keyTakeaways: The SEC filed a subpoena-enforcement lawsuit against ISS in Pennsylvania federal court after the proxy adviser allegedly failed to fully comply with a July 21 subpoena for voting records.

The action follows a December executive order from President Trump directing the SEC to tighten oversight of ISS and rival Glass Lewis, which together control more than 90% of the proxy-advisory market.
A 2025 court ruling had already vacated the SEC's prior proxy-adviser disclosure rules, leaving subpoena enforcement as one of the agency's few direct tools for the moment.

content.text: The Securities and Exchange Commission has escalated its scrutiny of the proxy advisory industry, filing a lawsuit against Institutional Shareholder Services to force the influential firm to hand over records the agency says it has withheld for months. The subpoena-enforcement action, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, marks one of the most direct regulatory confrontations yet in a broader campaign targeting the companies that shape how institutional investors vote their shares at annual meetings.

According to the SEC, its Division of Examinations opened a review of ISS in March and requested detailed information about the firm's voting recommendations and activity. When the agency concluded that ISS had not fully complied, its enforcement division issued a formal subpoena on July 21 seeking additional records; the SEC now says ISS has still not turned over everything requested, prompting the court filing.
A White House-driven campaign against proxy advisers

The lawsuit follows an executive order President Donald Trump signed in December, formally titled 'Protecting American Investors from Foreign-Owned and Politically-Motivated Proxy Advisors,' which directed the SEC to review its rules governing proxy advisers, more aggressively enforce existing securities-law antifraud provisions, and consider new disclosure and regulatory requirements for the industry. The order specifically named ISS and its chief rival, Glass Lewis, noting that the two firms together control more than 90% of the U.S. proxy-advisory market and directing federal agencies to examine whether their recommendations on matters tied to diversity, equity, and inclusion or environmental and social factors reflect political motivations rather than objective financial analysis.

Proxy advisers occupy an outsized role in corporate governance despite operating largely outside public view. Institutional investors managing thousands of portfolio companies rely on firms like ISS and Glass Lewis to research and recommend how to vote on matters ranging from board elections and executive pay packages to mergers and shareholder proposals, since evaluating every ballot item independently across a large portfolio would otherwise be impractical. That concentrated influence has made the firms a recurring target for critics, including some corporate executives who argue their recommendations can sway close votes without sufficient transparency into the methodology behind them.
A regulatory landscape already in flux

The SEC's legal fight arrives without a fresh rulemaking framework to lean on. A 2025 federal court ruling, later affirmed by the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, vacated the agency's prior rules governing proxy advisers, significantly narrowing its ability to mandate pre-dissemination disclosure requirements on firms like ISS. That leaves the current subpoena-enforcement action as one of the more direct tools available to regulators seeking greater visibility into how proxy advisers formulate their recommendations, rather than a broader rule change that would apply industry-wide.

ISS, which is registered with the SEC as an investment adviser, has not publicly detailed its reasons for resisting the subpoena, though the firm has previously argued that its voting recommendation methodologies constitute proprietary business information. The specifics of what the SEC is seeking remain under seal, but people familiar with the matter say the request centers on records covering roughly four years of client voting data and the firm's underlying recommendation criteria on matters including executive compensation and board elections.
What's at stake for investors and companies

The outcome of the case could carry implications well beyond ISS itself. A ruling favoring the SEC would likely set a precedent making it easier for regulators to compel similar information from other proxy advisers going forward, potentially reshaping how transparently these firms must operate. Corporate governance experts say increased scrutiny could push proxy advisers toward greater disclosure of their voting methodologies, which supporters argue would improve accountability, while critics worry it could also invite political pressure to shape recommendations in ways that move away from purely financial considerations.

For now, the case sits early in the litigation process, with the SEC asking the court simply to compel ISS's compliance with the outstanding subpoena rather than seeking penalties for any underlying violation. Legal observers expect the dispute, and the broader regulatory campaign around proxy advisers that has driven it, to remain a closely watched storyline for institutional investors and public companies alike as the 2027 proxy season approaches.

finance.metaTitle: Trump Claims 'Hundreds of Billions' in Stock Gains in AI-Generated Posting Spree
finance.title: Trump's Unverified Claim of 'Hundreds of Billions' in Stock Gains Draws Fresh Ethics Scrutiny
finance.metaDescription: President Trump's weekend Truth Social posting spree included an unsubstantiated claim of hundreds of billions of dollars in stock market gains, reviving questions about his personal trading activity and the paid Truth API service.
finance.excerpt: An unverified claim by President Trump that he made 'hundreds of billions' on stocks for the country has renewed scrutiny of his personal trading activity, disclosed financial holdings, and Truth Social's paid early-access feature.
finance.imageAlt: Stock market ticker display representing scrutiny of presidential trading claims and financial disclosures
keyTakeaways: President Trump claimed on Truth Social to have made 'Hundreds of Billions of Dollars' on stocks for the country, without providing supporting evidence for the figure.
Financial disclosures show Trump made more than 3,600 stock trades in the first quarter of 2026 alone, and he has not placed his assets in a blind trust.
The claim adds to scrutiny of Truth API, a $100,000-a-month feature giving paid subscribers early access to Trump's posts, which senators have asked the SEC to investigate.

content.text: President Donald Trump spent more than ten hours over the Labor Day weekend posting a stream of AI-generated images and sweeping financial claims on Truth Social, including an assertion that his investment decisions have earned the United States 'Hundreds of Billions of Dollars' on stocks and other holdings -- a claim that has drawn fresh scrutiny from ethics watchdogs and market observers who note the White House offered no supporting evidence.

Among the dozens of images the 80-year-old president shared during the extended posting spree was one depicting himself seated in front of stock-market monitors in the White House, captioned with the message that he undertakes the trading activity for the country rather than himself. The claim quickly drew skepticism from fact-checkers, who note that the largest documented gain the federal government has on record tied to any of Trump's investment-related actions is closer to $33 billion on paper, tied primarily to the U.S. government's roughly 10% equity stake in semiconductor giant Intel taken in August 2025 -- a stake now worth more than $50 billion given the run-up in Intel shares this year.
A pattern of market-moving posts

The posting spree adds to a broader pattern that has raised conflict-of-interest questions throughout Trump's second term. Financial disclosures reviewed by watchdog groups show the president engaged in more than 3,600 individual stock trades during just the first quarter of 2026 alone, totaling more than $100 million in trading volume, with over 1,000 additional trades recorded in June. Separate reporting has identified multiple instances in which Trump posted favorable commentary about specific companies on Truth Social shortly before purchasing shares in those same firms, though the president has maintained that his financial advisers direct all trading decisions independently of his public commentary.

Unlike most senior federal officials, sitting presidents are not legally barred from trading individual stocks while in office, and Trump has not placed his assets into a blind trust, an arrangement many of his predecessors used specifically to avoid the appearance of using privileged information for personal financial gain. Ethics experts say that combination leaves considerably more room for potential conflicts of interest than other officials face, particularly given the president's regular access to non-public policy deliberations capable of moving markets.
Scrutiny over Truth Social's paid early-access feature

The renewed attention to Trump's trading activity comes amid ongoing controversy surrounding Truth API, a $100,000-per-month subscription feature offered through Trump Media, the parent company of Truth Social, that gives paying subscribers faster access to the president's posts, including announcements about policy decisions capable of moving financial markets.
