content.text: A rapid rise for an infrastructure startup

Crusoe, a company that builds and operates data centers specifically designed to support AI computing workloads, has reached a valuation of thirty billion dollars in its latest funding round, marking one of the more striking valuation jumps among companies positioned in the physical infrastructure layer of the AI industry. The company's rise illustrates how investor enthusiasm for the AI boom has increasingly extended beyond model developers themselves to the specialized real estate, power and cooling infrastructure required to actually train and run large-scale AI systems.

Crusoe's business model has focused on developing data centers in locations with access to relatively low-cost or otherwise underutilized power sources, an approach the company says allows it to offer more competitive pricing to AI labs and cloud providers than facilities built in more traditional data center hubs where power availability has become increasingly constrained. That strategy has positioned the company as an attractive partner for AI labs racing to secure computing capacity amid an industry-wide infrastructure crunch.
Why investors are betting big

Venture investors involved in the latest funding round pointed to surging demand for AI training capacity as the primary driver behind the valuation increase, noting that data center capacity has become one of the most significant bottlenecks constraining how quickly AI labs can train and deploy increasingly large models. With major AI companies signing multi-year, multi-billion-dollar computing capacity agreements, infrastructure providers capable of delivering that capacity quickly and reliably have become unusually valuable in the current market environment.

Analysts note that the AI infrastructure buildout has increasingly resembled a capital-intensive arms race, with companies across the industry racing to secure land, power agreements and construction capacity years in advance of actual anticipated demand. That dynamic has created significant opportunities for well-capitalized infrastructure specialists like Crusoe, but it has also raised questions among some investors about whether the pace of data center construction could eventually outstrip actual long-term demand if AI adoption growth slows from its current trajectory.
Broader implications for the AI buildout

The funding round adds to a broader pattern of enormous capital flows into AI infrastructure companies this year, spanning chipmakers, data center developers, power generation partnerships and specialized cooling technology providers, all benefiting from what industry participants describe as an unprecedented buildout cycle. Some economists have begun drawing comparisons to prior infrastructure booms, cautioning that heavy capital investment cycles of this scale have historically been followed by periods of consolidation once initial demand projections are tested against reality.

For now, Crusoe says it plans to use the new funding to accelerate construction of several already-planned data center campuses and to expand its power procurement partnerships, positioning the company to compete for a growing pipeline of large-scale AI computing contracts. Industry watchers say the coming year will be a critical test of whether infrastructure valuations at this scale can be sustained as more capacity comes online across the sector.
A crowded field of infrastructure bets

Crusoe's valuation jump comes as a growing number of specialized AI infrastructure companies compete for a similar pool of investor capital and customer contracts, ranging from established data center real estate investment trusts expanding into AI-specific facilities to newer entrants focused exclusively on power procurement or advanced cooling systems needed for increasingly dense computing clusters. Investors say picking winners in this crowded field has become one of the more challenging exercises in venture capital given how quickly the underlying technology and customer requirements continue to evolve.

Company leadership has said Crusoe intends to differentiate itself through its focus on flexible, lower-cost power sourcing strategies rather than competing purely on scale with better-capitalized rivals, a positioning it believes will remain valuable even if overall AI infrastructure spending growth eventually moderates from its current exceptional pace. Whether that strategy proves durable is likely to become clearer over the next several quarters as more of the company's planned facilities move from construction into full operation.

investigation.metaTitle: Investigation: How Thousands of US Nursing Homes Keep Failing Minimum Staffing Rules — With Few Consequences
investigation.title: Investigation: How Thousands of US Nursing Homes Keep Failing Minimum Staffing Rules — With Few Consequences
investigation.metaDescription: A Northern Journal review of federal inspection records found a pattern of repeated staffing violations at nursing homes across the country, with penalties that rarely change underlying behavior.
investigation.excerpt: A Northern Journal review of federal inspection records found a pattern of repeated staffing violations at nursing homes across the country, with penalties that rarely change underlying behavior.
investigation.imageAlt: An elderly care facility hallway, representative of nursing homes across the United States
takeaways: Federal data shows a large share of US nursing homes fail to meet minimum daily staffing benchmarks.
Facilities cited for repeated violations frequently continue operating with only modest fines.
Industry groups say chronic underfunding and workforce shortages, not neglect, are driving the gap.

content.text: A pattern hidden in plain sight

A review of federal inspection data by The Northern Journal found that a significant share of nursing homes across the country have repeatedly failed to meet minimum daily staffing benchmarks set by federal regulators, even after being cited and, in some cases, fined for the same violations in prior inspection cycles. The pattern raises questions about whether the current system of penalties is strong enough to actually change behavior at facilities where understaffing has become a persistent, rather than occasional, problem.

Nursing homes that accept Medicare and Medicaid funding are required to maintain minimum levels of registered nurse and total nursing staff time per resident per day, standards designed to ensure residents receive adequate care for tasks ranging from medication management to help with basic daily activities like eating and bathing. Facilities that fall short can face fines, but inspectors and former regulators say the penalties are often modest relative to the cost of hiring and retaining sufficient staff, creating what some describe as a perverse financial incentive to accept fines rather than fully solving the underlying staffing gap.
What the data shows

Facilities cited multiple times for the same staffing deficiency were found across a wide range of states and ownership structures, including both for-profit chains and nonprofit operators, though the review found for-profit facilities were disproportionately represented among repeat violators. In many cases, the underlying deficiency reports described specific incidents in which residents experienced delayed care, including missed medication doses or delayed responses to call lights, that inspectors directly attributed to insufficient staff coverage on a given shift.

Former state health department surveyors who conduct these inspections said that while the citation process is designed to prompt corrective action plans, follow-up verification that staffing levels have genuinely improved can be inconsistent, particularly in states with their own surveyor staffing shortages. Some described a cycle in which facilities submit a corrective plan, pass a subsequent spot-check, and then staffing levels quietly slip again once the immediate regulatory attention has passed.
Industry pushes back

Nursing home industry associations have pushed back on characterizations that persistent understaffing reflects neglect, arguing instead that a nationwide shortage of nurses and certified nursing assistants, combined with reimbursement rates that have not kept pace with rising labor costs, makes meeting staffing benchmarks genuinely difficult for many facilities regardless of intent. Industry representatives say wages for nursing assistants in the sector often lag behind comparable jobs in retail or hospitality, making recruitment and retention an ongoing structural challenge rather than a simple matter of facility management choices.

Patient advocacy groups counter that whatever the underlying cause, the consequences for residents remain the same, and they have pushed for stronger, more consistently enforced penalties, including the potential loss of Medicare and Medicaid certification for facilities with a documented pattern of repeat violations. Several advocacy organizations have also called for greater public transparency, arguing that families searching for a nursing home for a loved one often have no easy way to see a facility's full staffing violation history before making a placement decision.
What comes next

Members of Congress on committees overseeing federal health programs have signaled interest in examining whether current penalty structures need to be strengthened, though any legislative changes would likely face pushback from industry groups warning that stricter penalties could force financially struggling facilities to close, reducing the overall supply of nursing home beds in already underserved areas. Regulators, for their part, say they are reviewing whether inspection follow-up procedures need to be tightened to ensure corrective actions are genuinely sustained rather than temporary fixes designed to pass the next scheduled inspection.

investigation.metaTitle: Investigation: Billions in Opioid Settlement Money Is Flowing Away From Addiction Treatment
investigation.title: Investigation: Billions in Opioid Settlement Money Is Flowing Away From Addiction Treatment
investigation.metaDescription: State and local governments received historic settlement payouts meant to address the overdose crisis. A Northern Journal review found a substantial share has gone to purposes with little direct connection to treatment or prevention.
investigation.excerpt: State and local governments received historic settlement payouts meant to address the overdose crisis. A Northern Journal review found a substantial share has gone to purposes with little direct connection to treatment or prevention.
investigation.imageAlt: A community naloxone and addiction support outreach table set up in a public space
takeaways: States and localities have received tens of billions of dollars from opioid manufacturer and distributor settlements.
A review of public spending disclosures found a meaningful share directed toward projects with limited connection to treatment.
Advocates say weak reporting requirements make it difficult to fully track how settlement money is actually used.

content.text: A historic settlement, an uneven spending record

State and local governments across the country have received tens of billions of dollars in settlement payments from opioid manufacturers, distributors and pharmacy chains found to have contributed to the overdose crisis, funds that were explicitly intended to expand addiction treatment, prevention and recovery services. A review of public spending disclosures by The Northern Journal found that while many jurisdictions have directed settlement funds toward their intended purpose, a meaningful share of the money has instead gone toward projects with only a loose or indirect connection to addiction treatment.

Examples identified in public budget documents included settlement funds used to cover general law enforcement equipment purchases, courthouse renovations and, in at least a handful of cases, expenses that appeared largely unrelated to substance use disorder services at all. Advocates who track settlement spending say the pattern reflects a structural weakness in how the funds were distributed, with many jurisdictions given significant discretion over spending decisions and comparatively limited reporting requirements to verify how the money is ultimately used.
Why oversight has been difficult

Unlike some prior public health settlements, the opioid settlement framework generally allows spending across a broad menu of approved categories, some of which are defined loosely enough to permit significant local discretion. Public health researchers say this flexibility was originally intended to let communities tailor spending to their specific local needs, since the nature and severity of the overdose crisis varies significantly between, for example, rural counties facing treatment facility shortages and urban areas dealing with fentanyl contamination in the illicit drug supply.

That same flexibility, however, has made independent oversight more difficult, since there is no single national database that allows the public to easily compare how similarly situated jurisdictions are spending their settlement dollars. Several states have set up their own public dashboards intended to improve transparency, though the level of detail and consistency of reporting varies considerably from state to state, and some local governments have faced criticism for delayed or incomplete public disclosures of their spending decisions.
Voices from the recovery community

Addiction treatment providers and recovery advocates say the gap between the settlement's intended purpose and some observed spending patterns is particularly frustrating given how severely underfunded treatment infrastructure remains in many parts of the country, with long waitlists for residential treatment beds and medication-assisted treatment programs common even in areas that received substantial settlement payouts. Some have called for state legislatures to adopt stricter statutory spending guardrails, arguing that voluntary guidance alone has proven insufficient to ensure funds are consistently directed toward evidence-based treatment and prevention programs.

Local officials defending their spending decisions have generally argued that categories like law enforcement equipment or drug-related court programs are legitimately connected to addressing the broader opioid crisis, even if they do not directly fund clinical treatment services, and some have noted that public health infrastructure investments can have longer-term benefits for prevention even when they are not immediately visible in overdose statistics. Public health researchers say resolving that disagreement will likely require clearer statutory definitions of eligible spending categories, an issue several state legislatures are expected to revisit as remaining settlement payments continue to be disbursed over the coming years.
Families affected by the crisis push for accountability

Families who lost loved ones to overdose deaths, some of whom were directly involved in the litigation that produced the settlements, say they feel a particular obligation to ensure the money is spent as intended, since the funds were secured specifically because of the harm caused to their communities. Several have formed advocacy groups specifically focused on monitoring local settlement spending, attending city council and county commission budget meetings to press for greater transparency and stronger accountability measures.

Legal experts who worked on the original settlement agreements say future legal action to enforce more specific spending requirements remains a theoretical possibility but would likely face significant hurdles, since the settlement terms were deliberately structured to give participating governments broad discretion in exchange for their agreement to resolve claims against the settling companies. Barring new legislation, they say, the primary check on how the money is spent will likely remain public pressure and transparency efforts rather than direct legal enforcement.

investigation.metaTitle: Investigation: Oversight Gaps Persist as ICE Detention Population Reaches Record Levels
investigation.title: Investigation: Oversight Gaps Persist as ICE Detention Population Reaches Record Levels
investigation.metaDescription: As the number of people held in immigration detention has climbed to historic highs, a Northern Journal review found that independent inspection capacity has not kept pace.
investigation.excerpt: As the number of people held in immigration detention has climbed to historic highs, a Northern Journal review found that independent inspection capacity has not kept pace.
investigation.imageAlt: A fenced facility exterior representative of immigration detention infrastructure in the United States
takeaways: The population held in US immigration detention has reached record levels this year.
Independent oversight and inspection capacity has not expanded at the same pace as the detained population.
Advocacy groups and some lawmakers are calling for expanded, standardized inspection requirements.

content.text: A record population, a strained inspection system

The number of people held in United States immigration detention facilities has climbed to record levels this year, driven by expanded enforcement priorities and increased detention capacity added through new and expanded facility contracts. A review by The Northern Journal of publicly available inspection reports and government watchdog findings shows that the independent oversight infrastructure responsible for monitoring conditions inside these facilities has not expanded at a comparable pace, raising concerns among advocacy groups and some lawmakers about whether adequate monitoring is occurring at the scale now required.

Detention facilities operate under a patchwork of oversight authorities, including internal agency inspections, contracted third-party audits and, in some cases, review by the Department of Homeland Security's own inspector general. Advocates who work directly with detained individuals say the frequency and rigor of these inspections varies considerably between facilities, and that some of the newer or rapidly expanded sites have not yet undergone the same level of scrutiny as longer-established facilities.
Findings from recent inspection reports

Publicly available inspection findings reviewed for this investigation described a range of recurring issues at various facilities, including delays in medical care access, concerns about food quality and sanitation, and inadequate access to legal counsel for detained individuals attempting to navigate complex immigration proceedings. Agency officials have generally disputed characterizations that conditions are systemically inadequate, pointing to internal standards that facilities are contractually required to meet and to corrective action processes triggered when deficiencies are identified.

Former facility monitors who have conducted site visits in the past say that even well-intentioned oversight mechanisms can struggle to keep pace when detained populations grow quickly, since thorough inspections require significant staff time and specialized expertise, particularly around medical care standards, that cannot simply be scaled up overnight. Some have called for Congress to mandate a minimum, standardized inspection frequency tied directly to facility population size, rather than the current system, which allows for greater administrative discretion in scheduling reviews.
Calls for expanded oversight

Immigration advocacy organizations have renewed calls for expanded, independent oversight mechanisms, including proposals to give congressional representatives and accredited legal observers more consistent, less restricted access to detention facilities in their districts. Some lawmakers have introduced legislation that would require more frequent, standardized public reporting of detention conditions data, though similar proposals in past sessions of Congress have not advanced to a floor vote.

Homeland Security officials maintain that existing oversight mechanisms are sufficient and note that facilities found to have serious, unresolved deficiencies can have their contracts terminated, pointing to a small number of facilities where that has occurred in recent years as evidence the system functions as intended. Advocacy groups counter that contract terminations remain relatively rare compared with the volume of documented deficiencies across the system, and they argue that more proactive, better-resourced oversight, rather than after-the-fact contract termination, is what is genuinely needed to ensure consistent conditions across a rapidly growing detention system.
Legal representation remains a persistent gap

Immigration attorneys say access to legal counsel remains one of the most consistently cited concerns across facilities of varying sizes and operators, since detained individuals facing complex immigration proceedings often have limited ability to secure private representation and no guaranteed right to a government-appointed attorney, unlike in the criminal justice system. Legal aid organizations serving detained populations say they are frequently stretched far beyond capacity relative to the number of people who need assistance navigating their cases.

Some members of Congress have proposed funding expanded legal orientation programs within detention facilities as a comparatively low-cost way to improve due process outcomes even if broader oversight reforms remain politically difficult to advance. Whether such proposals gain traction is likely to depend heavily on the outcome of broader immigration policy negotiations already underway in Congress this session.

investigation.metaTitle: Investigation: 'Forever Chemicals' Still Contaminate Drinking Water for Millions, Despite New Rules
investigation.title: Investigation: 'Forever Chemicals' Still Contaminate Drinking Water for Millions, Despite New Rules
investigation.metaDescription: Federal limits on PFAS in drinking water took effect with great fanfare. A Northern Journal review found many water systems are still years away from compliance, and some may never fully meet the standard.
investigation.excerpt: Federal limits on PFAS in drinking water took effect with great fanfare. A Northern Journal review found many water systems are still years away from compliance, and some may never fully meet the standard.
investigation.imageAlt: A municipal water treatment facility responsible for filtering drinking water for a community
takeaways: Federal limits on PFAS chemicals in drinking water are now in effect, but compliance timelines stretch years into the future.
A review found many water systems, particularly smaller ones, face significant cost and technical barriers to compliance.
Communities near industrial and military sites remain disproportionately affected by contamination.

content.text: New rules, a long road to compliance

Federal limits on per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, commonly known as PFAS or forever chemicals, in public drinking water systems are now formally in effect, marking a long-sought regulatory milestone for public health advocates who have pushed for stricter standards for years. But a review by The Northern Journal of water system compliance data found that a substantial number of water utilities, particularly smaller systems serving rural communities, remain years away from actually meeting the new standards, and some face genuine questions about whether full compliance is financially achievable without significant outside assistance.

PFAS chemicals, used for decades in products ranging from nonstick cookware to firefighting foam, are called forever chemicals because they break down extremely slowly in the environment and can persist in water supplies for years after the source of contamination is addressed. Exposure has been linked in scientific research to a range of health concerns, including certain cancers, immune system effects and developmental issues, prompting the new, more stringent federal limits after years of advocacy from affected communities and public health researchers.
The compliance gap

Water system operators say the primary barrier to faster compliance is cost, since removing PFAS from contaminated water supplies typically requires specialized filtration technology that can carry price tags well beyond what many smaller utilities, particularly those serving rural communities with a limited ratepayer base, can afford without substantial state or federal financial assistance. Larger urban water systems, with access to greater capital and technical expertise, have generally made faster progress toward compliance than their smaller counterparts.

Federal and state funding programs have been established to help offset compliance costs, including funds derived from legal settlements with chemical manufacturers found responsible for widespread PFAS contamination, but water utility associations say demand for that assistance far outstrips the funding currently available. Some smaller systems have applied for extensions or alternative compliance timelines allowed under the new rules, a process that public health advocates worry could leave some communities drinking water above the new health-based limits for years longer than intended.
Communities bearing the heaviest burden

Contamination levels remain disproportionately concentrated near current and former industrial facilities, military installations that historically used PFAS-containing firefighting foam, and airports, where affected communities have in many cases been aware of and organizing around contamination concerns for years before the new federal standards took effect. Residents in some of these communities say the new regulatory limits, while welcome, have done little to change their daily reality if their local water system has not yet completed the infrastructure upgrades needed to actually reduce contamination levels.

Environmental health advocates argue that the compliance timeline built into the new rules, while providing a necessary degree of practical flexibility for utilities facing genuine financial and technical constraints, risks becoming a de facto extension of harm for the communities already most affected by contamination. They are pushing for expanded, prioritized funding specifically targeted at the water systems facing both the highest contamination levels and the most limited financial capacity to address them, arguing that a one-size-fits-all national timeline does not adequately account for how unevenly both contamination and resources are currently distributed across the country.
Homeowners with private wells largely left out

The new federal standards apply specifically to public water systems, meaning the millions of American households that rely on private wells for their drinking water are not directly covered by the rule at all, even though private well contamination can occur in the same geographic areas affected by public system contamination. Public health officials generally recommend that private well owners near known contamination sources arrange independent testing, though the cost of both testing and any necessary treatment falls entirely on individual homeowners rather than being addressed through the public compliance framework.

Some states have begun offering testing assistance programs specifically for private well owners in areas near known contamination sources, but coverage remains inconsistent nationally. Advocates say closing this gap for private well households represents an important next step that has received comparatively little attention amid the broader public water system compliance debate.

investigation.metaTitle: Investigation: AI Data Centers Are Straining Local Water Supplies in Drought-Prone Communities
investigation.title: Investigation: AI Data Centers Are Straining Local Water Supplies in Drought-Prone Communities
investigation.metaDescription: As tech companies race to build the infrastructure powering the AI boom, a Northern Journal review found several facilities are drawing significant water for cooling in areas already facing scarcity concerns.
investigation.excerpt: As tech companies race to build the infrastructure powering the AI boom, a Northern Journal review found several facilities are drawing significant water for cooling in areas already facing scarcity concerns.
investigation.imageAlt: A large industrial cooling system used to regulate temperatures at a data center facility
takeaways: Large AI data centers can use millions of gallons of water daily for cooling, depending on their design.
Several facilities have been built in regions already facing water scarcity or drought conditions.
Local officials and residents are increasingly pushing back on water usage agreements they say lack transparency.

content.text: The hidden water cost of the AI boom

As technology companies race to build the enormous data centers needed to train and run increasingly powerful AI models, a review by The Northern Journal found that several major facilities have been constructed in regions already grappling with water scarcity concerns, raising questions from local officials and residents about whether adequate consideration was given to long-term water resource impacts during the permitting and approval process. Large data centers can use millions of gallons of water daily for cooling systems, depending on their specific design and the local climate.

Not all data centers rely equally on water for cooling, since some facilities use air-based or closed-loop cooling systems that consume significantly less water than traditional evaporative cooling towers. But the most computationally intensive AI training facilities, which generate enormous amounts of heat from densely packed processing hardware, have frequently favored water-intensive cooling approaches because they can be more energy-efficient and cost-effective to operate at scale, even though they carry a larger water footprint.
Communities raise concerns

In several communities where large data centers have been built or proposed, local residents and elected officials have raised concerns about water usage agreements they say were negotiated with limited public input or transparency about the actual volumes involved. In some cases, specific water allocation figures were only made public well after initial approvals had already been granted, following public records requests or local reporting that pressed utilities and technology companies for more detailed disclosures.

Local water utility officials in several affected areas have defended the agreements, noting that data center operators frequently pay premium rates for their water usage that can help fund broader infrastructure improvements benefiting the entire water system, and that companies have in some cases committed to water recycling or offset programs intended to reduce net impact. Critics counter that such offset commitments are difficult for the public to independently verify and that the underlying water usage still represents a meaningful new demand on regional supplies that were not necessarily planned for in long-term water resource management.
A patchwork of state responses

States have taken widely varying approaches to regulating data center water usage, with some requiring detailed water impact assessments as part of the permitting process and others leaving those decisions largely to local water utilities and municipal governments with limited state-level oversight. Some state legislatures have introduced bills this year specifically aimed at requiring greater transparency around large industrial water users, including data centers, though most such proposals remain in early stages of the legislative process.

Technology companies have generally emphasized their broader sustainability commitments and long-term investments in water-efficient cooling technology, arguing that newer facilities are increasingly designed with reduced water footprints compared with older data center generations. Even so, environmental researchers say the sheer pace of new data center construction driven by AI demand means water impact assessments and community engagement processes are struggling to keep up, a gap they argue needs to be addressed before, rather than after, new facilities are approved and built.
Farmers and municipal users compete for the same supply

In several agricultural regions where data centers have located near existing farmland, local farmers say they are increasingly concerned about competing for the same groundwater and surface water resources they rely on for irrigation, particularly during drought years when water allocation decisions become more contentious. Some agricultural associations have begun advocating for formal water rights protections specifically designed to prevent large industrial users from being prioritized over existing agricultural users during periods of scarcity.

Municipal water planners say balancing the economic development benefits data centers bring, including jobs and tax revenue, against long-term water resource sustainability has become one of the more difficult policy questions facing fast-growing regions, particularly as climate projections suggest drought conditions may become more frequent and severe in many of the same areas currently attracting the heaviest data center investment.

investigation.metaTitle: Investigation: Dark Money Groups Are Pouring Record Sums Into the 2026 Midterms — And Voters Often Can't Trace It
investigation.title: Investigation: Dark Money Groups Are Pouring Record Sums Into the 2026 Midterms — And Voters Often Can't Trace It
investigation.metaDescription: A Northern Journal review of campaign finance filings found a growing share of political spending this cycle is coming from groups that are not required to disclose their donors.
investigation.excerpt: A Northern Journal review of campaign finance filings found a growing share of political spending this cycle is coming from groups that are not required to disclose their donors.
investigation.imageAlt: Campaign advertising materials and mailers spread across a table during an election cycle
takeaways: Political spending from groups not required to disclose their donors has reached record levels this election cycle.
A Northern Journal review found dark money groups are especially active in a handful of the most competitive races.
Campaign finance reform advocates say voters are increasingly unable to trace who is funding the ads shaping their choices.

content.text: Untraceable money at record scale

Political spending from organizations not legally required to publicly disclose their donors has reached record levels heading into the 2026 midterm elections, according to a Northern Journal review of campaign finance filings and independent tracking data compiled by nonpartisan watchdog groups. The spending, often referred to as dark money because voters have no reliable way to trace its ultimate source, has become increasingly concentrated in the small number of House and Senate races both parties consider most likely to determine control of Congress.

Under current campaign finance law, certain categories of nonprofit organizations are permitted to spend money on political advertising and voter outreach without disclosing their individual donors, provided political activity does not become their primary purpose. Campaign finance experts say that legal framework, largely shaped by court rulings over the past two decades, has created an increasingly well-used pathway for wealthy individuals and organizations seeking to influence elections without having their identities publicly associated with specific campaigns or messages.
Where the money is going

The review found dark money spending concentrated heavily in a small number of battleground states, with advertising often focused less on directly promoting a specific candidate and more on shaping the broader narrative around contested issues like health care costs, immigration enforcement and economic policy in ways that indirectly benefit one party or candidate over another. Because these ads frequently avoid explicit candidate endorsement language, they can qualify for looser disclosure requirements than traditional campaign advertising while still meaningfully shaping how voters perceive the choices in front of them.

Campaign finance watchdogs say the practical effect is that voters in the most competitive districts are frequently exposed to a substantial volume of political messaging without any reliable way to know who is actually funding it or what interests might be motivating a particular message. Some of the largest dark money spending identified in the review has flowed through networks of interconnected nonprofit organizations, a structure campaign finance experts say can make it exceedingly difficult, even for dedicated investigative researchers, to fully trace the ultimate original source of funds.
Calls for reform meet familiar resistance

Campaign finance reform advocates have renewed calls for expanded disclosure requirements, arguing that voters have a fundamental right to know who is attempting to influence their vote, regardless of the specific legal structure through which the spending occurs. Legislation aimed at expanding disclosure requirements has been introduced in Congress in prior sessions but has consistently failed to overcome procedural hurdles, reflecting deep partisan disagreement over how to balance free speech considerations against transparency goals in campaign finance law.

Groups that rely on the current legal framework defend it as a legitimate exercise of constitutionally protected speech, arguing that mandatory donor disclosure could expose individuals and organizations to harassment or retaliation for supporting causes or candidates that prove unpopular in certain circles. With the framework unlikely to change before November, campaign finance trackers say they expect dark money spending to continue climbing as Election Day approaches, particularly in the small number of races both parties view as most likely to decide control of Congress.
State-level disclosure rules offer a partial patchwork

A handful of states have adopted their own stricter disclosure requirements for political spending that go beyond federal minimums, creating a patchwork in which the same organization might face different transparency obligations depending on which state a particular advertisement airs in. Campaign finance researchers say this state-level patchwork, while an improvement in the states that have adopted it, still leaves significant gaps given that federal races often involve national spending that crosses state lines in ways state-level rules cannot fully capture.

Some voting rights and transparency organizations have shifted focus toward pushing for stronger state-level rules as a more achievable near-term goal than federal reform, given the current gridlock in Congress on campaign finance legislation. Whether that strategy meaningfully reduces the overall opacity of political spending nationally remains an open question heading into the final stretch of the midterm campaign.

investigation.metaTitle: Investigation: Federal Food Safety Inspection Staffing Has Shrunk, Even as Outbreaks Rise
investigation.title: Investigation: Federal Food Safety Inspection Staffing Has Shrunk, Even as Outbreaks Rise
investigation.metaDescription: A Northern Journal review found inspector staffing levels have not kept pace with a growing and increasingly complex food supply chain, raising questions about the system's capacity to catch contamination before it spreads.
investigation.excerpt: A Northern Journal review found inspector staffing levels have not kept pace with a growing and increasingly complex food supply chain, raising questions about the system's capacity to catch contamination before it spreads.
investigation.imageAlt: A food processing facility where inspectors evaluate safety and sanitation standards
takeaways: Federal and state food safety inspection staffing has not kept pace with growth in the food supply chain.
A review found several recent outbreaks were linked to facilities that had gone extended periods without routine inspection.
Former officials warn the gap increases the risk that contamination is caught only after people are already sick.

content.text: A shrinking inspection workforce

Federal and state food safety inspection staffing levels have not kept pace with the growth and increasing complexity of the nation's food supply chain, according to a review by The Northern Journal of agency staffing data and inspection frequency records spanning the past several years. The gap has left a growing number of food processing and produce packing facilities going extended periods between routine inspections, a pattern former regulators say increases the risk that contamination issues are caught only after products have already reached consumers and, in some cases, made people sick.

Food safety inspections are intended to catch potential contamination risks, from improper sanitation practices to inadequate temperature controls, before products leave a facility and enter the broader supply chain. When staffing shortages stretch the time between inspections, former officials say problems that might otherwise be identified and corrected early can instead persist undetected until an outbreak investigation, often prompted only after people have already become ill, eventually traces contamination back to its source.
Tracing outbreaks back to inspection gaps

The review identified several recent multi-state foodborne illness outbreaks connected to facilities that inspection records show had gone significantly longer than the agency's own recommended inspection intervals between visits. In at least a few of these cases, follow-up inspections conducted only after an outbreak was already underway identified sanitation or process control issues that, food safety experts say, plausibly could have been caught and corrected earlier under a more consistent inspection schedule.

Agency officials have acknowledged staffing challenges but have pushed back on suggestions that current inspection frequency represents an acceptable public health risk, noting that facilities are also subject to their own internal quality control requirements and that the agency prioritizes inspection resources toward facilities and product categories considered highest risk based on past compliance history and the inherent characteristics of the products involved.
A workforce pipeline problem

Former agency officials describe a persistent difficulty recruiting and retaining qualified food safety inspectors, a specialized role requiring scientific training that can often command higher compensation in private sector quality assurance roles within the food industry itself. That competitive dynamic, combined with years of relatively flat federal budget allocations for inspection programs even as the volume and complexity of imported and domestically produced food has grown substantially, has left the inspection workforce increasingly stretched relative to its overall responsibilities.

Consumer safety advocates argue that food safety inspection funding should be treated as a public health investment with a clear return in prevented illness, hospitalization and lost economic productivity, rather than viewed primarily as a discretionary budget line subject to periodic cuts. With food safety funding levels once again part of the broader congressional appropriations negotiations already underway this fall, advocates say they are pushing hard for increased investment, though they acknowledge the outcome remains uncertain given the many competing budget priorities lawmakers are weighing simultaneously this cycle.
Technology as a partial stopgap

Some food safety officials point to expanded use of data analytics and predictive risk modeling as a way to at least partially offset reduced in-person inspection frequency, using historical compliance records and supply chain data to prioritize limited inspector time toward the facilities and product categories judged most likely to pose contamination risks. Critics of this approach caution that predictive models are only as good as the underlying data feeding them and cannot fully substitute for the kind of hands-on inspection that can catch unexpected or emerging risks a model was never trained to anticipate.

Industry groups have generally supported greater investment in inspection technology and staffing alike, noting that large-scale outbreaks are costly for food producers as well as consumers, both through direct recall expenses and longer-term reputational damage. That shared interest, some officials say, could provide a rare point of bipartisan and cross-industry agreement as budget negotiations continue this fall.

investigation.metaTitle: Investigation: Rural Hospital Closures Are Creating Growing 'Maternity Care Deserts' Across the US
investigation.title: Investigation: Rural Hospital Closures Are Creating Growing 'Maternity Care Deserts' Across the US
investigation.metaDescription: A Northern Journal review found a steady rise in the number of rural counties with no local hospital offering labor and delivery services, forcing many expectant mothers to travel long distances for care.
investigation.excerpt: A Northern Journal review found a steady rise in the number of rural counties with no local hospital offering labor and delivery services, forcing many expectant mothers to travel long distances for care.
investigation.imageAlt: A rural community hospital building serving a small town in the United States
takeaways: A growing number of rural counties have no hospital offering labor and delivery services.
Financial pressure and staffing shortages are the primary drivers cited for obstetric unit closures.
Expectant mothers in affected areas increasingly face long drives for prenatal care and delivery.

content.text: A growing gap in rural maternity care

A review by The Northern Journal of hospital service line data found a steady increase in the number of rural counties without a single hospital offering labor and delivery services, a trend commonly referred to as the growth of maternity care deserts that has left a growing share of rural expectant mothers facing significantly longer travel distances for prenatal care and delivery. The pattern has accelerated in recent years as financial pressure on rural hospitals, many already operating on thin or negative margins, has pushed administrators to close lower-volume, higher-cost service lines, with obstetric units frequently among the first to go.

Hospital administrators who have made the difficult decision to close obstetric units say the calculation is often unavoidable given the underlying economics, since labor and delivery services require maintaining specialized staff and equipment around the clock regardless of how many births actually occur in a given month, a cost structure that becomes increasingly difficult to sustain as rural populations age and birth rates in many rural counties continue to decline.
The human cost of longer travel distances

Public health researchers who study maternal health outcomes say longer travel distances to reach obstetric care have been associated with worse outcomes for both mothers and infants, including increased risk of complications during unplanned or emergency deliveries that occur before a mother can reach a distant hospital. Expectant mothers in affected rural communities describe having to plan delivery logistics, including where they will stay in the final weeks of pregnancy, well in advance given the significant travel distances now involved in some cases.

Rural health advocates note that the loss of local obstetric services often ripples beyond delivery itself, since many rural hospitals that close their labor and delivery units also see reduced availability of related prenatal and postpartum care locally, forcing pregnant patients to travel repeatedly throughout their pregnancy for routine appointments rather than only for the delivery itself. That cumulative travel burden, researchers say, can also contribute to reduced prenatal care utilization overall, a known risk factor for poorer maternal and infant health outcomes.
Policy responses under discussion

Federal and state policymakers have explored a range of potential responses, including enhanced Medicaid reimbursement rates specifically for rural obstetric services, grant programs aimed at helping struggling rural hospitals maintain labor and delivery units, and expanded support for midwifery and birth center models that can offer lower-cost alternatives to full hospital-based obstetric units in some communities. Rural hospital associations say that while these proposals could help at the margins, more fundamental reform of how rural hospitals are reimbursed for low-volume, high-fixed-cost service lines will likely be necessary to meaningfully reverse the broader trend.

For now, expectant mothers in an increasing number of rural counties continue to navigate a health care landscape reshaped by these closures, often relying on a combination of careful advance planning, family support networks and, in some cases, temporary relocation closer to a hospital in the final weeks of pregnancy. Advocates say the trend is likely to continue without significant policy intervention, given that the underlying financial pressures driving rural hospital service line closures show few signs of easing in the near term.
